title: The Tiger and the Mice
text: In a shady mango grove, a big tiger was sleeping under a tree.
A tiny mouse whispered, "Please let me pass, I need to gather fallen seeds."
The kind tiger opened his eyes and gently let the little mouse go.
Later that day, the tiger got his heavy paw caught in a hunter's net.
The brave mouse quickly chewed the ropes, freeing the tiger, and they became friends.
Both friends smiled happily, knowing that help can come from anyone, big or small.
This sweet story teaches us that true strength is always guided by kindness.
moral: Strength should be balanced with kindness.

title: The Crow and the Water Pot
text: On a sunny day, a thirsty crow found an earthen pot in a courtyard.
He peeked inside to drink, but the cool water was too far down.
Thinking fast, the clever crow began picking up small pebbles from the ground.
He dropped them into the pot one by one with his beak.
With each pebble, the water level rose higher and higher until it reached the top.
The happy crow drank all the water he wanted and flew away refreshed.
This smart bird teaches us that calm thinking can solve any hard problem.
moral: Cleverness must be used for good.

title: The Monkey and the Coconut
text: In a green coconut grove, a playful monkey found a ripe, brown coconut.
He tried hard to crack it open, but could not break the shell.
A friendly elephant walked by and offered to crack it with his strong trunk.
The joyful monkey thanked the gentle giant and shared the sweet coconut meat.
Together beneath the tall palm trees, the two friends enjoyed their jungle feast.
The little monkey smiled, thankful that he had asked for help when he needed it.
This cheerful tale reminds us that sharing with friends makes every treat taste sweeter.
moral: Playfulness can teach humility.

title: The Tortoise and the Hare
text: In a sunny green meadow, a speedy hare loved boasting about how fast he ran.
A patient, quiet tortoise smiled and challenged the speedy hare to a race.
The hare dashed far ahead and stopped to sleep beneath a cool banana leaf.
The steady tortoise kept walking step by step without stopping or looking back.
When the lazy hare woke up, the tortoise was already crossing the finish line!
All the jungle animals cheered as the humble tortoise won the grand race.
This famous story reminds us that slow and steady effort always wins in the end.
moral: Every creature has a lesson to teach.

title: The Fox and the Grapes
text: A clever fox was strolling through a fruit garden when he saw purple grapes.
The juicy bunch hung high above, and his mouth watered just looking at them.
He leaped high into the air again and again, but could not reach them.
Tired and out of breath, he finally gave up and turned his nose up.
"Those grapes are probably sour anyway!" the fox muttered as he walked away.
He pretended he did not care, though he really wished he could eat them.
This funny story shows how people pretend to dislike what they cannot get.
moral: Cunning alone is not enough without honesty.

title: The Wolf And The Kid
text: A little goat with tiny new horns thought he was already big and brave.
When the herd started home, his mother called, but he did not listen.
He kept eating the soft grass until he looked up and saw no one around.
The little goat was completely alone in the wide, empty pasture.
The warm golden sun was setting quietly behind the hills.
Long, dark shadows began creeping over the quiet grassy ground.
A cool evening breeze rustled the grass with scary whistling sounds.
The little goat shivered with fear as he remembered the fierce wolf.
He began running across the open field, crying out loudly for his mother.
Suddenly, right beside a bunch of trees, the hungry wolf appeared!
The frightened little goat knew that he could not run away in time.
"Please, Mr. Wolf," he pleaded, "I know you want to eat me up."
"Before you do, please play a merry tune on your flute so I can dance!"
The wolf liked the idea, so he played a tune while the goat danced happily.
Meanwhile, the herd of goats was walking slowly toward the village.
The sound of the wolf's flute music traveled far across the quiet fields.
The brave shepherd dogs heard the music and pricked up their ears.
Knowing that a wolf was near, the fierce dogs raced back to the pasture.
The wolf dropped his flute and fled, wishing he had never stopped to make music!
moral: Do not let anything turn you from your purpose.

title: The Tortoise And The Ducks
text: As you know, the slow tortoise always carries his hard shell on his back.
No matter where he goes, he can never leave his little home behind.
Old tales say the king of gods gave him this shell for being too lazy.
After many long years, the lonely tortoise wished he could travel and see new places.
He watched the birds fly happily and rabbits hop swiftly through the green grass.
He wished with all his heart to explore the wide world like other animals.
One morning, he met two friendly ducks by the pond and shared his wish.
"We can help you see the world from above," the kind ducks said.
"Bite this wooden stick tightly, and we will carry you up into the blue sky."
"Just remember to keep your mouth closed, or you will fall down!"
The excited tortoise agreed gladly and gripped the center of the stick tightly.
Each duck held an end, and together they flew high up into the clouds.
A black crow flying by looked up at the floating tortoise in great surprise.
"Look! That must surely be the grand King of all the Tortoises!" the crow called.
"Of course I am!" the proud tortoise shouted out, opening his mouth wide.
He lost his grip, fell from the sky, and crashed onto the rocks.
moral: Foolish curiosity and vanity often lead to misfortune.

title: The Young Crab And His Mother
text: "Why do you always walk sideways like that?" asked a mother crab by the sea.
She scolded her little son as they crawled across the warm wet sand.
"You should always walk straight forward with your claws pointing outward nicely."
"Please show me how, dear mother," the little crab answered politely, "I want to learn."
So the mother crab tried with all her might to walk straight ahead.
Try as she might, she could only scuttle sideways across the sandy beach.
When she tried turning her feet straight, she tripped over her own claws and fell!
moral: Do not tell others how to act unless you can set a good example.

title: The Frogs And The Ox
text: A big ox walked down to a grassy village pond to drink cool water.
Stepping heavily into the mud, his huge hoof accidentally crushed a tiny frog.
Soon, Mother Frog returned and asked the others where the little one was.
"A giant monster with huge feet stepped on our brother!" one frog cried.
"A giant, was he?"
asked Mother Frog, taking a deep breath and puffing herself up round.
"Was this monster as big as I am right now?"
"Oh, much bigger!"
all the little frogs cried out together.
Mother Frog sucked in more air and puffed herself up even rounder.
"He could not possibly be bigger than this!" she insisted proudly.
The little frogs shouted "Bigger!", so she puffed harder until she suddenly burst!
moral: Do not attempt the impossible.

title: The Dog, The Cock, And The Fox
text: A loyal dog and a colorful rooster were best friends who lived on a farm.
One morning, they decided to walk down a forest trail to see new places.
The two cheerful friends walked along happily, enjoying the cool breeze and leafy trees.
When evening fell, the rooster looked for a safe branch where he could sleep.
The dog crawled inside a cozy hollow tree trunk, and the rooster flew up high.
Both friends slept soundly and peacefully under the shining stars until the morning.
At the very first light of dawn, the rooster woke up bright and early.
For a moment, he forgot that he was sleeping in the middle of a forest.
He thought he was back home, waking the village families at sunrise.
He flapped his colorful wings and crowed loudly into the morning air.
Instead of waking the farmers, his loud cry woke a hungry fox nearby.
The fox licked his lips greedily, dreaming of a delicious morning breakfast.
Rushing over to the tree, he bowed politely and called up to the rooster.
"Welcome to our forest, handsome bird! I am so delighted to hear your lovely voice!"
"Please come down so that we can become the dearest of lifelong friends."
The clever rooster saw through the trick and replied with a calm smile.
"Knock on the door at the tree trunk, and my guard will let you in."
The greedy fox ran around the trunk, and the dog jumped out and caught him!
moral: Those who try to deceive may expect to be paid in their own coin.

title: Belling The Cat
text: The little mice held a meeting to find safety from the scary cat.
They wanted a warning whenever she walked nearby so they would have time to run.
They lived in constant fear of her sharp claws and rarely left their tiny holes.
Many clever ideas were shared, but none of them seemed practical enough to work.
At last, a young mouse stood up proudly and said, "I have a simple plan!"
"All we have to do is tie a small bell around the cat's neck."
"Whenever the bell jingled, we would hear her coming and scurry into our holes!"
All the little mice clapped and cheered, overjoyed by such a brilliant idea.
Then, a wise old grandfather mouse slowly stood up and asked a quiet question.
"A clever plan indeed, but tell me: who will bell the cat?"
moral: It is one thing to say that something should be done, but quite a different matter to do it.

title: The Eagle And The Jackdaw
text: A mighty eagle swooped down, caught a lamb, and flew to her nest.
A silly crow watched and thought he was strong enough to do the same.
Flapping his black wings with a fierce look, he swooped onto a big woolly ram.
He tried to fly, but his claws got tangled in the thick wool.
The big ram did not even feel the tiny bird on his back.
The village shepherd saw the fluttering bird and ran over with a cheerful grin.
He caught the fluttering crow and clipped his wings to keep him safe.
That evening, the shepherd took the funny bird home to show his happy children.
"What an unusual, funny little bird this is!" the children laughed together.
"Father, what do you call this little winged creature?" they asked curiously.
"This is only a little jackdaw crow, my dear children," the father replied.
"Though in his own proud mind, he truly believes he is a mighty eagle!"
moral: Do not let your vanity make you overestimate your powers.

title: The Boy And The Filberts
text: A little boy was allowed to reach into a narrow clay jar of tasty nuts.
Greedily, he grabbed the biggest fistful he could, filling his hand completely.
His full fist got stuck tightly in the narrow neck of the jar.
He was unwilling to drop even one nut, yet he could not free his hand.
Upset and crying, he burst into tears because his hand was trapped inside.
"Take half the nuts, dear son, and your hand will slide out easily."
moral: Do not attempt too much at once.

title: Hercules And The Wagoner
text: A farmer was driving his heavy bullock cart along a muddy road after a rainstorm.
The wheels sank deep into the thick mud, and the cart stopped completely.
The lazy farmer climbed down, staring at the stuck wheels without even trying to push.
He simply cried about his bad luck and begged the mighty hero Hercules for help.
Hercules appeared and said, "Put your shoulder to the wheel and push your cart!"
"Do you think this cart will move just by crying over it?"
"Help only comes to those who first make an honest effort to help themselves!"
The farmer pushed hard, the horses pulled, and the cart rolled out easily!
moral: Self help is the best help.

title: The Kid And The Wolf
text: A lively little goat was placed safely on the thatched roof of a village barn.
Looking down from the roof, he saw a wolf and mocked him rudely.
The calm wolf replied, "Your harsh words do not bother me at all."
"It is the high roof that speaks so bravely today, not your own little heart!"
moral: Do not say anything at any time that you would not say at all times.

title: The Town Mouse And The Country Mouse
text: A city mouse traveled out to a quiet green village to visit her country cousin.
For lunch, the country mouse served fresh wheat grains, tender roots, and cool river water.
The city mouse nibbled tiny bites politely, showing that she found the food very plain.
After lunch, the city mouse talked endlessly about all the grand luxuries back in town.
That night, they slept comfortably together inside a cozy little nest beneath the bushes.
The village mouse dreamed of delicious city treats and shiny palaces all night long.
The next morning, the village mouse happily packed her bag to visit the big city.
Inside the grand mansion, they found delicious leftovers from a rich banquet on the table.
There were sweet cakes, fresh breads, honey treats, and rich yellow cheese everywhere.
As the village mouse ate, a scary cat scratched loudly at the door!
Terrified, both mice dashed into a dark hole in the wall, hardly daring to breathe.
When they tiptoed back out, a loud barking house dog burst into the dining room!
The frightened village mouse grabbed her little bag and rushed straight toward the open door.
"You may keep your grand feasts! I prefer my peaceful village life without constant fear!"
moral: Poverty with security is better than plenty in the midst of fear and uncertainty.

title: The Fox And The Grapes
text: A hungry fox walked through an orchard and spotted ripe grapes hanging high.
The juicy grapes looked sweet and fresh, making the fox's mouth water with longing.
The grapes hung high on a branch, so he had to jump.
He leaped high into the air, but missed them by a long way.
He took a few steps back and ran forward for another leap, but missed again.
He jumped again and again, but the grapes stayed out of reach.
Tired and panting, he sat on the grass, staring up in disgust.
"I am wasting my time! Those grapes are sour and not worth eating!"
With his nose in the air, he walked away, pretending not to care.
moral: There are many who pretend to despise and belittle that which is beyond their reach.

title: The Bundle Of Sticks
text: An old village father had sons who were always arguing and fighting each other.
Words never helped, so he decided to teach them an important practical lesson.
After another loud quarrel, he asked his sons for a bundle of sticks.
He tied the sticks together and asked each son to break the bundle.
Each boy tried his best, but none could break the tied bundle.
Then the father untied the string and handed each son a single thin stick.
Snap! Each boy broke his single stick in two with no effort at all.
"My sons, when you stay united and help each other, no enemy can defeat you."
"If you stay divided, you will be broken easily like these single sticks."
moral: In unity is strength.

title: The Wolf And The Crane
text: A greedy wolf ate too fast, and a bone stuck in his throat.
He could neither cough nor swallow, and was in terrible pain.
Being unable to eat was a terrible trouble for such a greedy wolf.
So he ran through the forest to find a graceful crane standing by the river.
Her long neck and slender beak could reach inside to pull it out.
"I will give you a wonderful gift if you pull out this bone."
The crane was very nervous about putting her head inside a scary wolf's mouth.
But wanting the promised prize, she reached inside and pulled the sharp bone free.
Feeling completely relieved of his pain, the wolf turned around and began walking away.
"Wait! What about my promised reward?"
the crane called out after him anxiously.
"What!" the wolf snarled fiercely, turning around with a wicked grin.
"Have you not already received your great reward today?"
"You took your head out of my mouth safely without me biting it off!"
moral: Expect no reward for serving the wicked.

title: The Ass And His Driver
text: A donkey walking down a steep hill foolishly decided to take a dangerous shortcut.
Seeing his stable below, he thought jumping off the cliff was the fastest way.
His master caught his tail, but the stubborn donkey pulled toward the edge.
"Very well, go your own stubborn way and see what happens to you!"
The master let go, and the silly donkey tumbled headfirst down the hill!
moral: They who will not listen to reason but stubbornly go their own way against the friendly advice of those who are wiser than they, are on the road to misfortune.

title: The Oxen And The Wheels
text: Two patient oxen were pulling a heavy wooden cart along a muddy village road.
They used all their strength to pull the load, but they never made a complaint.
But the noisy wheels on the wooden cart behaved very differently the whole time.
Even though rolling was easy work, the wheels creaked and groaned loudly with every turn.
The hardworking oxen struggled through thick mud while listening to the wheels complain constantly.
Hearing that endless whining made the long journey feel even heavier and harder to bear.
"Quiet down back there!" the tired oxen called out at last in deep frustration.
"Why are you wheels complaining so noisily at every turn of this road?"
"We are pulling all the heavy weight, yet we work quietly without saying a word!"
moral: They complain most who suffer least.

title: The Lion And The Mouse
text: A mighty lion was sleeping peacefully, his big head resting on his paws.
A timid little mouse ran across his nose in the grass, trying to scurry away.
Waking from his nap, the angry lion caught the tiny creature under his heavy paw.
"Please spare me!" begged the mouse. "Let me go, and I will help you!"
The lion laughed out loud, amused that a tiny creature thought she could help him.
But feeling kind-hearted, he lifted his giant paw and let the little mouse run free.
Days later, the lion was caught in a hunter's strong rope net.
Unable to free himself, his loud, angry roars echoed all through the deep forest.
The mouse recognized his voice and quickly ran to find the lion trapped in ropes.
She gnawed through the thick rope with her sharp teeth until the lion was free.
"You laughed when I promised help," the proud little mouse said with a smile.
"Now you see that even a tiny mouse can save a mighty king of beasts!"
moral: A kindness is never wasted.

title: The Shepherd Boy And The Wolf
text: A young shepherd boy watched over a flock of sheep near a quiet village.
Day after day, watching the grazing animals felt very boring to the restless boy.
To pass the time, he would talk to his dog or play his flute.
Sitting by the trees, he thought of a naughty trick to have some exciting fun.
The village elders had told him to shout if a wolf attacked the flock.
So, without seeing any wolf, he ran toward the houses shouting loudly, "Wolf!
Wolf!" The worried villagers dropped their tools and rushed quickly to help the boy.
But when they arrived out of breath, they found him laughing at his silly trick.
A few days later, the foolish boy cried out again, "Wolf! Wolf! Save me!"
Once again the villagers ran to help, only to be laughed at by the boy.
Then one evening at sunset, a real, fierce wolf jumped out from the bushes!
In sheer terror, the trembling boy ran toward the village shouting, "Wolf!
Wolf!" But though the villagers heard his frantic cries, they refused to run this time.
"He cannot fool us again with his silly lies," they said, staying right at home.
The wolf chased the scattered sheep away, and the weeping boy learned a painful lesson.
moral: Liars are not believed even when they speak the truth.

title: The Gnat And The Bull
text: A tiny fly buzzed noisily across the grassy field and rested on a bull's horn.
After resting his wings for a little while, he prepared to fly away again.
Before leaving, the proud little fly spoke grandly to the big, strong bull.
"You must be so relieved that I am finally leaving your heavy horn," he buzzed.
"It makes no difference to me at all," the bull replied calmly without looking up.
"I did not notice when you arrived, nor will I care when you leave."
moral: The smaller the mind the greater the conceit.

title: The Plane Tree
text: Two tired travelers walked under the hot afternoon sun and rested beneath a big tree.
Looking up into the cool green branches, they saw it was a shady Plane Tree.
"What a useless tree this is!" one of the ungrateful men said with a sigh.
"It bears no sweet fruit to eat, and only drops dry leaves on the ground."
"Ungrateful travelers!"
whispered a gentle voice rustling through the green leaves of the Plane Tree.
"You rest safely in my cool shade, yet you call me completely useless!"
"O king of gods, see how people so easily forget the blessings they receive!"
moral: Our best blessings are often the least appreciated.

title: The Farmer And The Stork
text: A gentle, trusting stork was invited by a flock of cranes to visit a field.
The visit brought trouble when all the birds got trapped in a net.
Caught tightly in the ropes, the frightened stork begged the farmer to spare him.
"Please let me go, kind farmer!" the gentle stork pleaded with tears in his eyes.
"I belong to an honest bird family, and I have always been a good bird."
"I did not even know that the cranes came here to steal your seeds!"
"You may be innocent, but you chose bad friends and must share their fate."
moral: You are judged by the company you keep.

title: The Sheep And The Pig
text: One day, a shepherd found a little fat pig wandering in his sheep pasture.
He caught the pig, who immediately began squealing at the top of his voice.
Hearing the loud noise, you would think the pig was being badly hurt.
The shepherd held the wriggling pig firmly and walked off toward the village market.
The amused sheep followed to the gate, wondering why the pig made such noise.
"Why do you scream and cry like that?" one gentle sheep asked curiously.
"The shepherd often catches and carries one of us away in his arms too."
"Yet none of us makes such a loud fuss or cries like a baby!"
"That is easy for you to say," the pig replied with another frantic kick.
"When he catches you, he is only looking for your warm winter wool."
"When he catches me, he wants my life! Oink! Oink! Oink!"
moral: It is easy to be brave when there is no danger.

title: The Travelers And The Purse
text: Two men were walking together along a road when one found a heavy purse.
"How lucky I am!" he cheered. "I have found a bag of money!"
"It feels very heavy, so it must be full of shiny gold coins."
"Do not say 'I found it,'" his friend said, "say 'we found it together.'"
"True friends who travel together should share both good luck and bad luck."
"No way!" the greedy man snapped. "I found it, so it is mine alone!"
Just then, loud angry voices shouted down the road, "Stop that thief! Catch him!"
Looking back, they saw an angry crowd running toward them carrying wooden sticks.
The man holding the money bag began trembling with fear and panic.
"We are ruined if the villagers find this stolen purse with us!" he cried.
"Do not say 'we,'" his companion replied calmly, "you must say, 'I am ruined!'"
moral: We cannot expect any one to share our misfortunes unless we are willing to share our good fortune also.

title: The Lion And The Ass
text: As a majestic lion walked down a forest path, all the animals bowed respectfully.
But a silly donkey stood nearby and brayed a rude remark as he passed.
The lion felt a flash of anger and turned his head to see who spoke.
Seeing only a foolish donkey, the noble king calmly walked on, ignoring him completely.
moral: Do not resent the remarks of a fool. Ignore them.

title: The Frogs Who Wished For A King
text: A pond of frogs grew tired of their peaceful and quiet lives.
They did nothing but croak lazily, wishing for a grand king to rule them.
"We want a mighty king with pomp and power!" they declared out loud.
So they prayed to the king of gods, begging him to send a royal ruler.
The king of gods dropped a huge log, which splashed loudly into the water.
The frightened frogs hid under the lily pads, thinking he was a terrifying giant.
But soon, they saw that King Log was completely quiet, peaceful, and harmless.
Young frogs dove off him, and old frogs sat on him complaining about him.
To teach them a lesson, the ruler of gods sent a hungry crane instead.
King Crane was very different indeed from the peaceful wooden log they had disliked.
He quickly began gobbling up frogs one by one, filling them with terror!
In weeping croaks, the surviving frogs begged the king of gods to save them.
"Are you still not happy with your new king?" the god replied sternly.
"You asked for this ruler, so you have only yourselves to blame today!"
moral: Be sure you can better your condition before you seek to change.

title: The Owl And The Grasshopper
text: An owl always took her deep sleep during the bright daytime hours.
At sunset, as shadows spread through the woods, she blinked and flew out.
Her loud "Hoo-hoo!" echoed as she hunted for beetles, frogs, and little mice.
As she grew older, this grumpy owl became very annoyed by daytime noise.
One warm afternoon, a green grasshopper nearby began a loud, screeching song.
Out popped the owl's head from the round hollow inside the big oak tree.
"Go away from here, little singer!" she called down to the grasshopper.
"Have you no manners? Please let an old bird sleep in peace and quiet!"
But the rude grasshopper replied that he had every right to sing in the sunshine.
Then he rubbed his wings and chirped even louder to annoy the owl.
The clever owl knew that arguing with a stubborn creature would never work.
Besides, her eyes were not sharp enough in bright daylight to catch him.
So she hid her anger and spoke to him with sweet, gentle words.
"Well sir," she cooed, "since I am awake, let me enjoy your lovely song."
"I have delicious honey nectar here, like the sweet drink the music god loves."
"Please hop up into my hollow and share this sweet treat with me."
"It will make your singing voice sound sweeter than music from the sky!"
The proud, foolish grasshopper believed the owl's flattering words and hopped right up.
But as soon as he came close, the old owl pounced and swallowed him whole!
moral: Flattery is not a proof of true admiration.

title: The Wolf And His Shadow
text: A hungry wolf stepped out of his den feeling very proud and fierce.
The setting sun cast a giant shadow of him that stretched across the ground.
"Look at me!" the wolf gasped proudly. "I am a hundred times bigger now!"
"Why should a giant beast like me ever run from a little lion?"
Suddenly a huge shadow covered him, and a real lion knocked him down instantly!
moral: Do not let your fancy make you forget realities.

title: The Oak And The Reeds
text: A giant oak tree stood near a quiet stream where slender green reeds grew.
When breezes blew, the oak stood stiff and tall, holding its branches skyward.
Down below, the slender reeds bowed low in the wind, swaying very softly.
"You have good reason to complain," the proud oak tree said to them.
"A tiny breeze bends you, while I stand firm against every wild storm."
"Do not worry about us," the gentle reeds whispered back with a smile.
"The blowing wind does not harm us when we sway along with it."
"We bend before the winds, and that is why we never break."
"You stand stiffly against every gust in all your pride and stubborn strength."
"One day, a storm may be too strong for your stiff trunk."
Just then, a mighty windstorm rushed fiercely through the dark forest trees.
The oak stood stiffly fighting the gale, while the slender reeds bent low.
Crack! The fierce storm snapped the giant oak, crashing him down beside the reeds.
moral: Better to yield when it is folly to resist, than to resist stubbornly and be destroyed.

title: The Rat And The Elephant
text: A little gray rat was scampering proudly along the king's wide royal highway.
Even though he was tiny, he was full of foolish and boastful pride.
Walking along the road edge, he heard music as a royal parade arrived.
It was the great king traveling with all his royal guards and followers.
The king rode upon a giant elephant decorated with shiny cloths and bells.
Sitting beside the king in a grand seat was the royal pet cat.
A big crowd of happy villagers followed behind, cheering and waving their hands.
Everyone cheered for the magnificent elephant, completely ignoring the little rat down below.
Seeing this, the proud little rat felt deeply hurt and very upset.
"What silly fools you all are!"
he squeaked out angrily at the top of his lungs.
"Look at me, and you will forget that clumsy gray elephant right away!"
"Are you amazed only because he is so big and heavy to see?"
"Or do you like him just for his wrinkly skin and trunk?"
"I have bright eyes, two ears, and four legs just like him!"
"I am just as important as—" But the cat pounced, and the rat scampered away!
moral: A resemblance to the great in some things does not make us great.

title: The Boys And The Frogs
text: Some village boys were playing happily by the edge of a freshwater pond.
For fun, they began throwing flat stones to skip across the pond water.
The stones flew fast and splashed everywhere, frightening a family of green frogs below.
At last, the oldest and bravest frog poked his head above the water.
"Please stop throwing stones, dear children; what is fun for you hurts us deeply!"
moral: Always stop to think whether your fun may not be the cause of another's unhappiness.

title: The Crow And The Pitcher
text: During a dry summer, a thirsty crow searched everywhere for a cool drink.
He found a tall clay pot with a little water at the bottom.
The pot had a narrow neck, so the crow could not reach inside.
Sitting patiently, a clever and wonderful idea popped into his sharp little mind.
He picked up small pebbles one by one and dropped them inside the pot.
With every pebble, the water rose until the clever crow could drink happily!
moral: In a pinch a good use of our wits may help us out.

title: The Ants And The Grasshopper
text: On a sunny autumn morning, hardworking ants were busy drying their stored grain.
A hungry grasshopper with a fiddle arrived, begging humbly for a bite to eat.
"What!" cried the ants in surprise. "Did you not store any food for winter?"
"What on earth were you doing all through the warm summer months?"
"I was too busy making cheerful music," the grasshopper whined sadly with a sigh.
"Making music all summer, were you?" the busy little ants replied with a frown.
"Now go dance all winter!" they said, turning back to their important work.
moral: There's a time for work and a time for play

title: The Ass Carrying The Image
text: A sacred statue of a deity was being carried to the village temple.
It was placed upon a donkey decorated with flower garlands and bright cloths.
As they walked, respectful people bowed their heads low before the holy statue.
The foolish donkey thought all the people were bowing down to honor him!
Full of silly pride, he stopped in the street and began braying loudly, "Hee-haw!"
His driver saw what the silly donkey was thinking and tapped him firmly.
"Keep moving, silly donkey! The people bow to the statue, not to you!"
moral: Do not try to take the credit to yourself that is due to others.

title: A Raven And A Swan
text: A Raven, who was as black as coal, was very jealous of the Swan, because her feathers were as white as fresh snow.
The foolish Raven thought that if he lived like the Swan, swimming and eating water plants all day, his feathers would also turn white.
So he left his home in the woods and went to live near the lake and the marshes.
But no matter how much he washed and splashed all day long, his feathers stayed as black as before.
The water plants did not suit him at all, so he grew thinner and thinner, and at last he died.
moral: A change of habits will not alter nature.

title: The Two Goats
text: Two Goats were happily jumping on the rocky slopes of a mountain. They met each other, one on each side of a deep gap with a fast river rushing below.
A fallen tree trunk was the only way to cross the gap. It was so narrow that even two squirrels would find it hard to pass each other safely.
The path was thin and scary. But the two Goats were not afraid at all.
Neither Goat wanted to step aside for the other. Both were too proud to give way.
One Goat stepped onto the log. The other stepped on too.
They met right in the middle, horn to horn. Neither would move back, and so they both tumbled into the roaring river below.
moral: It is better to yield than to come to misfortune through stubbornness.

title: The Ass And The Load Of Salt
text: A merchant was taking his donkey home from the seaside. The donkey was carrying a very heavy load of salt.
They had crossed that river many times before without any trouble. But this time the donkey slipped and fell in the middle of the river.
When the merchant finally got the donkey back on its feet, much of the salt had melted away in the water.
The donkey felt how much lighter the load was now. He was very happy and finished the journey with a spring in his step.
The next day, the merchant went back for another load of salt.
This time the donkey remembered what had happened at the river. So he fell into the water on purpose to melt the salt again.
The angry merchant turned around right away. He took the donkey back to the seaside and loaded him with two big baskets full of sponges.

At the river, the donkey fell in again. But when he got up, the sponges had soaked up all the water and were ten times heavier than before. The sad donkey dragged himself home with a much bigger load.
moral: The same measures will not suit all circumstances.

title: The Lion And The Gnat
text: Go away, you tiny bug! shouted a Lion angrily at a Gnat that was buzzing around his head.
But the Gnat was not scared at all.
Do you think I am afraid of you just because they call you king? the Gnat said boldly to the Lion.
The very next moment the Gnat flew at the Lion and stung him hard on the nose.
The Lion was furious. He struck at the Gnat again and again but only hurt himself with his own claws.
The Gnat kept stinging the Lion, who was now roaring very loudly.
At last, tired out and covered in wounds he had made himself, the Lion gave up the fight.
The Gnat flew off, wanting to tell everyone about his great win. But instead he flew straight into a spider's web.
And so the tiny bug who had beaten the King of all animals met a sad end, caught by a little spider.
moral: The least of our enemies is often the most to be feared.

title: The Leap At Rhodes
text: A man had visited many faraway places. When he came back home, all he could talk about were his great deeds abroad.
One of his favourite stories was about a huge jump he had made in a city called Rhodes.
He said the jump was so enormous that no one else in the world could jump anywhere near as far.
He also said that many people in Rhodes had seen him do it and could prove he was telling the truth.
No need for witnesses, said one of his listeners. Pretend this village is Rhodes.
Now show us how far you can jump!
moral: Deeds count, not boasting words.

title: The Cock And The Jewel
text: A rooster was busily scratching the ground, looking for food for himself and his family. While digging, he turned up a precious jewel that someone had lost.
Ah! said the rooster. You must be very costly and the person who lost you would be very happy to find you.
But as for me, I would choose a single grain of rice over all the jewels in the world!
moral: Precious things are without value to those who cannot prize them.

title: The Monkey And The Camel
text: At a grand celebration for King Lion, the Monkey was asked to dance for everyone.
The Monkey danced beautifully, and all the animals cheered and praised him greatly.
All the praise made the Camel very jealous.
He was sure he could dance just as well. So he pushed through the crowd and stood up on his back legs to dance.
But the big clumsy Camel looked very silly as he kicked out his knobbly legs and twisted his long neck around.
The other animals kept jumping away from his huge, heavy hooves.
When one of his enormous feet came close to King Lion's nose, the animals were so upset that they chased the Camel far away into the desert.
Soon after, refreshments made mostly from the Camel were served to the company.
moral: Do not try to ape your betters.

title: The Wild Boar And The Fox
text: A Wild Boar was sharpening his tusks on the stump of a tree when a Fox happened to pass by.
Now the Fox always liked to make fun of others.
So he started looking around nervously, pretending he was scared of some hidden danger.
But the Boar just kept on sharpening his tusks without stopping.
Why are you doing that? asked the Fox at last with a grin. I cannot see any danger anywhere.
That is true, replied the Boar. But when danger does come, I will not have time to do this.
My weapons must be ready to use, or I will be in big trouble.
moral: Preparedness for war is the best guarantee of peace.

title: The Ass, The Fox, And The Lion
text: A Donkey and a Fox had become very good friends. They went everywhere together.
While the Donkey ate fresh green plants, the Fox would grab a chicken from a nearby farm or some food from the village.
One day the two friends suddenly came face to face with a Lion.
The Donkey was very frightened, but the Fox told him not to worry.
I will talk to the Lion, said the Fox. He walked right up to the Lion boldly.
Your Highness, the Fox whispered so the Donkey could not hear, I have a plan. If you promise not to hurt me, I will lead that foolish Donkey into a pit where he cannot escape, and you can eat him.
The Lion agreed, and the Fox went back to the Donkey.
I have made the Lion promise not to hurt us, said the Fox. Come, I know a good place to hide until he is gone.
So the Fox led the Donkey into a deep pit.
But when the Lion saw that the Donkey was trapped, he first of all pounced on the cheating Fox.
The Fox who had betrayed his friend was punished first.
And the Donkey who had trusted a traitor was left to face the Lion alone.
moral: Traitors may expect treachery.

title: The Birds, The Beasts, And The Bat
text: The Birds and the Beasts declared war against each other.
There was no making up, and so they fought with all their might.
The fight had started because the Fox family kept chasing and eating the Geese.
The Beasts also had their reasons to fight.
The Eagle kept swooping down on Hares, and the Owl ate Mice every single day.
It was a terrible war.
Many Hares and many Mice were killed.
Chickens and Geese fell in large numbers, and the winner always stopped to feast.
Now the Bat family had not clearly joined either side.
They were very clever and sneaky about it.
When they saw the Birds winning, they pretended to be Birds and joined the Birds.
But when the Beasts started winning, they quickly switched sides and joined the Beasts.
When the war ended, everyone talked about what the Bats had done.
Such cheating was unforgivable, and both Birds and Beasts came together to drive the Bats away.
And that is why, even today, Bats hide in dark towers and empty old buildings, only coming out at night.
moral: The deceitful have no friends.

title: The Lion, The Bear, And The Fox
text: Just as a Bear rushed to grab a young goat, a Lion leaped from the other side to grab the same animal.
The two fought hard for the prize. They hurt each other so badly that both fell down, too weak to go on.
Just then a Fox came running, grabbed the young goat, and ran off as fast as he could. The Lion and the Bear could only watch helplessly.
How much better it would have been, they said sadly, if we had shared it like friends.
moral: Those who have all the toil do not always get the profit.

title: The Wolf And The Lamb
text: One early morning, a little Lamb stood drinking water on the bank of a stream in the forest.
That very same morning, a hungry Wolf came by higher up the same stream, looking for something to eat.
He soon spotted the Lamb.
Normally the Wolf would have grabbed such a tasty meal without any fuss. But this Lamb looked so small and helpless that the Wolf felt he needed some excuse to eat it.
How dare you splash around in my stream and stir up all the mud! he roared angrily.
You deserve to be punished for being so careless! But please, do not be angry, said the shaking Lamb. I could not possibly muddy your water.
Remember, you are drinking higher up the stream, and I am drinking lower down.
The water flows from you to me, not the other way.
You are muddying it! the Wolf snarled. And besides, I heard you told lies about me last year!
How could I have done that? said the poor Lamb.
I was not even born last year!
Well then, it was your brother!
I have no brothers.
Then it was someone in your family, growled the Wolf. No matter who it was, I am not going to miss my breakfast.
And with no more talk, the Wolf grabbed the poor little Lamb.
He carried her off into the forest.
moral: The unjust will not listen to the reasoning of the innocent.

title: The Wolf And The Sheep
text: A Wolf had been badly hurt in a fight with a Bear.
He could not move and was very hungry and thirsty.
A Sheep walked past near his hiding place, and the Wolf called out to her.
Please bring me a drink of water, he begged. It will give me strength so I can find some solid food.
Solid food! said the Sheep.
You mean me, I suppose.
If I brought you a drink, it would only wash me down your throat.
No thank you — I will not bring you a drink!
moral: A knave's hypocrisy is easily seen through.

title: The Hares And The Frogs
text: Hares are very timid animals. Even the smallest shadow makes them run away and hide in fear.
One day they were so tired of being scared all the time that they decided they would rather die than live this way.
But while they were still talking about it, they heard a noise and in a flash they all ran back to their burrows.
On the way, they passed a pond where a family of Frogs was sitting among the reeds on the bank.
The moment the Frogs heard the Hares coming, they leapt into the mud in fright.
Look! cried a Hare. Things are not so bad for us after all — there are creatures who are even more frightened of us!
moral: However unfortunate we may think we are there is always someone worse off than ourselves.

title: The Fox And The Stork
text: The Fox thought of a plan to make fun of the Stork, whose long beak always made the Fox laugh.
Please come and have dinner with me today, said the Fox to the Stork, already smiling to himself about the trick he was planning.
The Stork was very happy to accept and arrived on time with a good appetite.
The Fox served soup, but he put it in a very flat, shallow bowl. The Stork could only just dip the very tip of his long beak in it, and could not drink any soup at all.
The Fox lapped it up easily and pretended to enjoy it very much, making the Stork feel even worse.
The hungry Stork was upset by the trick, but he was calm and did not want to get into a fight.
So, not long after, he invited the Fox to come and eat at his home.
The Fox came on time and smelt a very tasty fish dinner.
But the Stork served the food in a tall jar with a very narrow neck.
The Stork easily ate with his long beak, but the Fox could only lick the outside of the jar and sniff the lovely smell.
When the Fox became upset, the Stork said calmly, Do not play tricks on others unless you can take the same treatment yourself.
moral: Do not play tricks on your neighbors unless you can stand the same treatment yourself.

title: The Travelers And The Sea
text: Two travellers were walking by the seashore. Far out in the water they saw something floating on the waves.
Look! said one of them. A great ship is coming from far away, carrying rich treasures!
The floating object slowly came closer and closer.
No, said the other traveller. That is not a treasure ship. That must be a fisherman's small boat, carrying a fresh catch of fish.
The object kept coming nearer. The waves slowly pushed it up to the shore.
It must be a chest of gold from a shipwreck! they both cried out excitedly.
Both travellers ran to the beach as fast as they could.
But when they got there, all they found was a heavy, wet log.
moral: Do not let your hopes carry you away from reality.

title: The Wolf And The Lion
text: A Wolf had stolen a little Lamb and was carrying it off to his den to eat.
But his plans changed when a Lion blocked his path. Without any excuses, the Lion simply took the Lamb away from him.
The Wolf moved to a safe distance and then cried in an injured voice, You have no right to take what is mine!

The Lion looked back. The Wolf was too far away to be taught a lesson easily. So the Lion said calmly, Your property? Did you buy it? Did the shepherd give it to you as a gift? Tell me, how exactly did you get it?
moral: What is evil won is evil lost.

title: The Stag And His Reflection
text: A Stag was drinking from a clear spring and saw his own reflection in the water.
He greatly admired his beautiful antlers but felt very ashamed of his thin, spindly legs.
Why do I have such weak legs, he sighed, when I have such a magnificent crown on my head?
Just then he smelled a Panther nearby and instantly bounded away through the forest.
But as he ran, his wide antlers got caught in the branches of the trees, and the Panther quickly caught up with him.
Too late, the Stag understood that the legs he was ashamed of could have saved his life, but the grand antlers he was so proud of had been his downfall.
moral: We often make much of the ornamental and despise the useful.

title: The Peacock
text: Long ago, the Peacock did not have the beautiful feathers he is so proud of today.
One day, he begged the goddess Juno, who loved him dearly, to give him a grand tail to make him stand out from all the other birds. She granted his wish.
Dressed in his shining feathers of green, gold, purple, and blue, he strutted proudly among the birds.
All the birds envied him. Even the most beautiful pheasant had to admit the Peacock looked more splendid.
One day the Peacock saw an Eagle soaring high up in the bright blue sky. He felt like flying too, just as he used to do.
He spread his wings and tried to lift off from the ground.
But the weight of his heavy, magnificent tail pulled him back down.
Instead of soaring up to meet the morning sun or gliding through golden clouds at sunset, he was now stuck walking on the ground, more weighed down than any ordinary farmyard bird.
moral: Do not sacrifice your freedom for the sake of pomp and show.

title: The Mice And The Weasels
text: The Weasels and the Mice were always fighting each other.
In every battle, the Weasels won and also carried off many Mice to eat for their dinner.
The Mice held a big meeting and decided their army kept losing because they had no leaders.
So they chose the bravest and most important Mice to be generals and commanders.
To look different from the other Mice, these new leaders put fancy feather and straw decorations on their heads.
After training hard for a long time, the Mouse army sent a challenge to the Weasels.
The Weasels were very happy to accept the challenge — they loved a fight when a meal was at stake.
The Weasels attacked the Mouse army with great numbers.
Soon the Mice could not hold on, and the whole army ran away looking for holes to hide in.
The ordinary Mice slipped easily into their small holes, but the Mouse leaders could not fit through the narrow openings because of their big head decorations.
Not a single leader escaped from the hungry Weasels.
moral: Greatness has its penalties.

title: The Wolf And The Lean Dog
text: A Wolf was wandering near a village one evening when he came across a Dog.
It was a very thin and bony Dog. The Wolf would usually have walked away from such a poor meal, but he was very hungry that day.
So the Wolf began to creep toward the Dog, while the Dog slowly backed away.
Please, your honour, said the Dog, dodging the Wolf's snapping teeth, think about how unpleasant it would be to eat me right now. Just look at my ribs — I am all skin and bone!
But let me tell you a secret.
In a few days, my master will hold a big feast at our house for his daughter's wedding.
Imagine how fat and plump I will be after eating all those feast leftovers!
That is the right time to eat me! The Wolf liked the idea of a fat, juicy Dog very much.
So he walked away, tightening his belt and promising to come back later.
Some days later the Wolf returned, ready for his promised meal.
He found the Dog safely inside his master's courtyard and called out to him to come out.
Sir, said the Dog with a big smile, I will be very happy to come out for you to eat me.
Just wait until the gatekeeper opens the gate for me.
But the gatekeeper was a huge and fierce Dog that the Wolf knew very well and was very afraid of.
So the Wolf decided not to wait and ran away as fast as his legs could carry him.
moral: Do not depend on the promises of those whose interest it is to deceive you.

title: The Fox And The Lion
text: A very young Fox who had never seen a Lion before happened to meet one in the forest.
One look at the Lion was enough. The Fox ran away as fast as he could to the nearest hiding place.
The second time the Fox saw the Lion, he stopped behind a tree to peek at him for a moment before quietly sneaking away.
But the third time, the Fox walked straight up to the Lion without any fear and said cheerfully, Hello there, old friend!
moral: Acquaintance with evil blinds us to its dangers.

title: The Lion And The Ass
text: A Lion and a Donkey agreed to go hunting together.
While searching for animals, they spotted some Wild Goats running into a cave. They made a plan to catch them.
The Donkey would go inside the cave and make loud noises to scare the Goats out, while the Lion would wait at the entrance to catch them.
The plan worked perfectly. The Donkey made such a terrible racket inside the cave, kicking and braying loudly, that the Goats rushed out in panic and ran straight into the Lion.
The Donkey came out of the cave feeling very proud of himself.
Did you see how I made them run? he said happily.
Yes, indeed, said the Lion. And if I had not known you, I would surely have run away too!
moral: The loud-mouthed boaster does not impress nor frighten those who know him.

title: The Dog And His Master'S Dinner
text: A Dog had learned to carry his master's dinner to him every day.
He was very faithful to his job, even though the lovely smell of the food tempted him greatly.
The other Dogs in the neighbourhood noticed him carrying the basket and soon found out what was inside.
They tried many times to steal the basket from him.
But he always guarded it faithfully.
Then one day all the neighbourhood Dogs got together and blocked his path on the way.
The Dog tried to run away from them.
But then he made the mistake of stopping to argue with them.
That was his big mistake.
They teased and mocked him so much that he dropped the basket and grabbed a big piece of roasted meat meant for his master.
Fine then, he said. You all divide the rest.
moral: Do not stop to argue with temptation.

title: The Vain Jackdaw And His Borrowed Feathers
text: A Jackdaw was flying over the garden of the King's palace one day.
There he saw a flock of beautiful Peacocks in all their colourful glory and felt very jealous.
Now the Jackdaw was a plain black bird and not very graceful in his ways.
But he thought that all he needed was to dress like a Peacock and then he could live among them.
So he gathered some feathers that the Peacocks had dropped and stuck them among his own black feathers.
Dressed in his borrowed finery, he strutted proudly in front of his own bird friends.
Then he flew down into the garden to join the Peacocks.
But the Peacocks saw through the trick very quickly.
Angry at the cheat, they plucked away the borrowed feathers and some of his own too.
The sad Jackdaw flew back to his own friends.
But another nasty surprise was waiting for him there.
They remembered how he had acted too good for them, and they chased him away with pecks and jeers to punish him.
moral: Borrowed feathers do not make fine birds.

title: The Monkey And The Dolphin
text: Once upon a time, a ship sailing toward a great city was caught in a terrible storm and sank near the shore.
Luckily, some kind Dolphins were nearby. They were great friends of people and came to the rescue, carrying the sailors safely to shore on their backs.
The Dolphins swam hard and brought the people to safety on the beach.
In those days, people liked to take their pet monkeys and dogs along with them on their sea voyages.
One Dolphin spotted a Monkey struggling in the water and thought it was a person. He asked the Monkey to climb onto his back.
Then the Dolphin swam toward the shore with the Monkey on his back.
The Monkey sat very still and serious on the Dolphin's back, trying to look important.
Are you from this great city? asked the Dolphin politely.
Oh yes, replied the Monkey proudly. My family is one of the most important families in the city.
Really! said the Dolphin. Then you must visit the port often.
Oh yes, yes! said the Monkey. The port is my very best friend!
The Dolphin was very surprised by this strange answer. He turned his head and saw that he was carrying a Monkey, not a person.
Without wasting another moment, the Dolphin dived under the water and left the foolish Monkey to look after himself, while he swam off to find a real person to save.
moral: One falsehood leads to another.

title: The Wolf And The Ass
text: A Donkey was grazing in a field near the forest when he noticed a Wolf hiding in the shadows by the hedge.
He easily guessed what the Wolf was planning and quickly thought of a way to save himself.
So he pretended to be hurt and began to limp as if he was in great pain.
When the Wolf came up, he asked what had hurt the Donkey. The Donkey said he had stepped on a sharp thorn.
Please pull it out, he begged, groaning loudly. If you eat me with the thorn still in my hoof, it might get stuck in your throat.
The Wolf thought this was very wise advice. He did not want to choke on his meal.
So the Donkey lifted his foot and the Wolf bent down very carefully to look for the thorn.
At that moment the Donkey kicked out with all his strength and sent the Wolf flying many steps away.
While the Wolf lay on the ground, slowly and painfully getting back up, the Donkey galloped away to safety.
Serves me right, growled the Wolf as he crept away into the bushes.
I am a hunter, not a doctor.
I should stick to what I know.
moral: Stick to your trade.

title: The Monkey And The Cat
text: Once upon a time, a Cat and a Monkey lived together as pets in the same house.
They were great friends and were always getting into mischief together.
What they loved most of all was finding something tasty to eat, and they did not care much how they got it.
One day they were sitting by the fireplace, watching some chestnuts roasting in the hot coals.
They both wanted the chestnuts but did not know how to get them out of the fire.
I would happily get them, said the clever Monkey, but you are so much better at these things than me. Why don't you pull them out and I will share them between us?
The Cat carefully reached out her paw, pushed some ash aside, and pulled her paw back quickly.
She tried again and managed to hook a chestnut halfway out of the fire.
A third time, she pulled a chestnut out fully.
She did this again and again, burning her paw badly each time.
Each time she pulled a chestnut out, the Monkey popped it straight into his mouth.
Just then their master walked in and both rascals ran off. The poor Cat had a burnt paw and no chestnuts at all.
After that day, it is said, the Cat decided she was better off catching mice and rats, and had very little to do with the Monkey.
moral: The flatterer seeks some benefit at your expense.

title: The Dogs And The Fox
text: Some Dogs found the skin of a Lion lying on the ground and began to tear at it angrily with their teeth.
A Fox happened to walk by and laughed at them with scorn.
If that Lion were still alive, he said, the story would be very different.
You would quickly find out how much sharper his claws are than your teeth!
moral: It is easy and also contemptible to kick a man that is down.

title: The Dogs And The Hides
text: Some hungry Dogs saw some animal skins lying at the bottom of a river, where a leather-worker had left them to soak.
A nice skin would have made a great meal, but the water was deep and the Dogs could not reach the skins from the bank.
So they held a meeting and decided that the best plan was to drink up the whole river.
They all started lapping up the water as fast as they could.
They drank and drank until, one by one, each Dog had drunk so much that it burst. But even after all that effort, the water in the river was just as high as before.
moral: Do not try to do impossible things.

title: The Rabbit, The Weasel, And The Cat
text: A Rabbit left his burrow one day to go and eat some clover in the field.
But he forgot to latch his door, and while he was away a Weasel walked right in and made himself comfortable at home.
When the Rabbit came back, he found the Weasel's nose poking out of his own doorway, sniffing the fresh air.
The Rabbit was very upset and asked the Weasel to leave.
But the Weasel was very happy where he was. He had no plans to go anywhere.
A wise old Cat nearby heard the argument and offered to settle it.
Come closer to me, said the Cat. I am very hard of hearing. Both of you put your mouths close to my ears and tell me what happened.
The trusting pair did as they were told. In an instant, the Cat had both of them under her claws.
No one could argue that the matter had been very firmly settled.
moral: The strong are apt to settle questions to their own advantage.

title: The Bear And The Bees
text: A Bear was wandering through the forest looking for berries when he came upon a fallen tree where a swarm of Bees had stored their honey.
The Bear sniffed carefully around the log to see if the Bees were home.
Just then one Bee came flying back from the field, carrying a load of sweet nectar.
The Bee guessed what the Bear was up to. It flew at the Bear, stung him sharply on the nose, and then disappeared inside the hollow log.
The Bear was furious. He attacked the log with his teeth and claws, trying to smash the nest.
But this brought the whole swarm of Bees rushing out at once.
The poor Bear had to run away as fast as he could, and could only escape by jumping into a pool of water.
moral: It is wiser to bear a single injury in silence than to provoke thousand by flying into a rage.

title: The Fox And The Leopard
text: A Fox and a Leopard were resting lazily after a big meal and began arguing about who looked better.
The Leopard was very proud of his shiny, spotted coat and said that the Fox looked quite plain and ordinary.
The Fox was proud of his fluffy tail with its white tip, but he knew he could not beat the Leopard in looks.
Still, the Fox kept on talking with sharp and clever words, just for the fun of the argument.
The Leopard was about to lose his temper when the Fox yawned and got up.
You may have a very fine coat, said the Fox. But you would be much better off with a little more smartness inside your head, and a little less show on your body — the way I have it.
Now that is what I call real beauty.
moral: A fine coat is not always an indication of an attractive mind.

title: The Heron
text: A Heron was walking slowly along the bank of a stream, watching the clear water with his sharp eyes. His long neck and pointed beak were ready to snap up something tasty for breakfast.
The water was full of fish, but the Heron was very fussy that morning.
No small fish for me, he said to himself.
Such tiny creatures are not good enough for a great bird like me.
A lovely young fish swam close by.
No, no, said the Heron with a shake of his head.
I would not even bother to open my beak for something that small!
As the sun got warmer, the fish moved away from the shallow water near the bank and swam down to the cooler, deeper parts of the river.
The Heron could find no more fish at all, and was finally very glad to eat just a tiny snail for his breakfast.
moral: Do not be too hard to suit or you may have to be content with the worst or with nothing at all.

title: The Cock And The Fox
text: One lovely evening as the sun was setting, a wise old Rooster flew up into a tree to sleep for the night.
Before he settled down, he flapped his wings three times and crowed loudly.
But just as he was about to tuck his head under his wing, his sharp little eyes caught a flash of red and the pointy nose of a Fox standing right below him.
Have you heard the wonderful news? called the Fox in a very excited and happy voice.
What news? asked the Rooster very calmly. But deep inside he felt a little flutter of fear, for he was quite afraid of the Fox.
He was always a little worried when the Fox was nearby.
Your family and mine and all the animals have made a deal to forget all our fights and live together in peace and friendship forever!
Just think of it! I cannot wait to give you a big hug!
Please come down, dear friend, and let us celebrate this happy day together!
How wonderful! said the Rooster. I am truly delighted to hear such news!
But he said it in a dreamy way, standing on his tiptoes and staring at something far in the distance.
What are you looking at? asked the Fox, a little nervously.
Why, it looks like a couple of Dogs running this way.
They must have heard the good news too and But the Fox did not wait to hear the rest.
He turned and ran away fast. Wait! cried the Rooster.
Why are you running? The Dogs are your friends now!
Yes, yes, called the Fox over his shoulder. But they might not have heard the news yet. And besides, I just remembered a very important errand I must do right away!
The Rooster smiled to himself, tucked his head under his wing, and went peacefully to sleep. He had cleverly tricked a very cunning enemy.
moral: The trickster is easily tricked.

title: The Dog In The Manger
text: A Dog was sleeping in a manger full of hay. He was woken up by the Cattle, who came in tired and very hungry after a long day of work in the fields.
But the Dog would not let them near the manger. He growled and snapped at them as if the hay were the most delicious food in the world, all meant just for him.
The Cattle looked at the Dog with great disgust. How selfish he is! said one of them.
He cannot eat the hay himself, and yet he will not let us eat it when we are so hungry!
Just then the farmer walked in.
When he saw what the Dog was doing, he picked up a stick and chased the Dog out of the stable with many a hard smack, to punish him for his selfish ways.
moral: Do not grudge others what you cannot enjoy yourself.

title: The Wolf And The Goat
text: A hungry Wolf saw a Goat eating grass on top of a steep cliff, where he could not possibly reach her.
That looks very dangerous up there! he called out, pretending to be very worried about the Goat's safety. What if you fall? Please listen to me and come down!
There is the most wonderful, soft, fresh grass right here for you.
The Goat looked down at him from the cliff.
How very, very worried you are about me! she said with a knowing look.
And how kind of you to offer your grass! But I know you well. You are not thinking about my safety at all — you are only thinking about your own empty stomach!
moral: An invitation prompted by selfishness is not to be accepted.

title: The Ass And The Grasshoppers
text: One day a Donkey was walking in a field when he came across some Grasshoppers chirping away happily in a grassy corner.
He listened with great wonder and admiration to their cheerful singing.
It was such a joyful sound that the Donkey's heart filled with a great wish to sing just like them.
What is it that gives you such a beautiful voice? he asked them very respectfully.
Is there some special food you eat, or some magic drink that makes you sing so wonderfully?
Yes! said the Grasshoppers, who loved a good joke. It is the morning dew we drink! Try some and see!
From that day on, the foolish Donkey ate nothing and drank nothing but dew.
Of course, the poor Donkey soon became very weak and died.
moral: The laws of nature are unchangeable.

title: The Mule
text: A Mule had rested for a long time and eaten lots of good food.
He felt very strong and proud. He pranced around with his head held high.
My father was surely a great racehorse, he said to himself.
I can feel it in my bones! But the next day he was put back to work, and that evening he felt very sad.
I was wrong, he said quietly.
My father was just a donkey after all.
moral: Be sure of your pedigree before you boast of it.

title: The Fox And The Goat
text: A Fox fell into a well. It was not very deep, but he could not climb out.
After a long time, a thirsty Goat came walking by.
The Goat thought the Fox had gone down to drink. He asked if the water was good.
The best water in the whole land! said the clever Fox. Jump in and try it. There is plenty for both of us!
The thirsty Goat jumped right in and began to drink.
Quick as a flash, the Fox jumped onto the Goat's back and leaped out of the well using the Goat's horns.
The poor Goat now saw what trouble he was in. He begged the Fox to help him out.
But the Fox was already running away into the forest.
If you had as much sense as you have beard, old friend, he called back, you would have thought of a way out before you jumped in!
moral: Look before you leap.

title: The Cat, The Cock, And The Young Mouse
text: A very young Mouse went out into the world for the first time. He nearly got into big trouble!
He ran back home and told his mother everything that had happened.
I was walking along happily, he said, when I turned into the next yard and saw two very strange creatures.
One of them looked very kind and gentle. But the other one was the most frightening thing I had ever seen!
You should have seen him! On his head and neck hung pieces of bright red skin.
He stomped around, scratching the ground with his feet and beating his sides with his wings.
The moment he saw me, he opened his sharp beak wide and let out a loud, scary cry. I ran away as fast as I could!
Can you guess which animal the little Mouse was talking about?
It was a Rooster — the first one the young Mouse had ever seen!
If it had not been for that scary creature, said the Mouse, I would have gone to meet the other one. He looked so sweet and gentle.
He had soft, thick fur, a calm face, and bright, shining eyes.
He was waving his long, fluffy tail at me and seemed to be smiling.
I think he was just about to speak to me, when the scary one let out a loud screech and I ran away!
My dear son, said the Mother Mouse, that gentle creature you liked is the Cat.
Under his soft and sweet look, he wants to eat every one of us.
The scary one was just a Rooster. He would never hurt you. The Cat eats us! Be glad you are safe, my child, and always remember — never judge anyone by their looks.
moral: Do not trust alone to outward appearances.

title: The Wolf And The Shepherd
text: A Wolf had been watching a flock of Sheep for a long time. The Shepherd kept a close eye on him to keep the lambs safe.
But the Wolf did not try to hurt anyone. He even seemed to help the Shepherd look after the Sheep.
After many days, the Shepherd got used to seeing the Wolf around. He forgot how dangerous the Wolf could be.
One day the Shepherd left his flock with the Wolf and went away on an errand.
When he came back, he saw that many sheep had been killed and taken away. He knew then how foolish it was to trust a Wolf.
moral: Once a wolf, always a wolf.

title: The Peacock And The Crane
text: A Peacock, very full of pride, met a Crane one day. He spread out his beautiful tail feathers in the sunlight to show off.
Look at me! he said. What do you have that is as grand as this?
I am dressed in all the colours of the rainbow! Your feathers are as grey as dust!
The Crane spread his wide wings and flew up high toward the sky.
Follow me if you can! he called. But the Peacock stayed down below with the other yard birds, while the Crane flew freely far up into the blue sky.
moral: The useful is of much more importance and value, than the ornamental.

title: The Farmer And The Cranes
text: Some Cranes saw a farmer ploughing a big field.
They watched patiently as he sowed the seeds.
What a feast this will be for us! they thought.
As soon as the Farmer went home, the Cranes flew down and began eating the seeds as fast as they could.
The Farmer knew about Cranes and their habits.
He had dealt with such birds before.
He soon came back to the field with a sling.
But he brought no stones with him.
He thought he could scare the Cranes just by swinging the sling and shouting loudly.
At first the Cranes flew away in a great fright.
But soon they saw that none of them ever got hurt.
They did not even hear stones flying through the air. Loud words alone could not harm them.
After a while, they paid no attention to the Farmer at all.
The Farmer knew he had to do something more.
He wanted to save at least some of his grain.
So he put real stones in his sling and hit several Cranes.
That did the trick! The Cranes never came back to his field again.
moral: Bluff and threatening words are of little value with rascals.

title: The Farmer And His Sons
text: An old farmer knew he did not have many more days to live. He called his sons to his bedside.
My sons, he said, listen carefully to what I tell you.
Do not sell our family's land. It has been ours for many, many years.
Somewhere on this land, there is a great treasure hidden.
I do not know exactly where it is, but it is there. You will find it if you search well.
Do not give up. Dig every part of the land with all your strength.
The father passed away. As soon as he was gone, the sons began to dig the land with all their might. They dug up every corner of the farm, two or three times over.

They found no gold hidden anywhere. But when harvest time came and they counted their earnings, they had made much more money than any of their neighbours. Then they understood — the treasure their father spoke of was the rich crop that grew from their hard work.
moral: Industry is itself a treasure.

title: The Two Pots
text: Two pots stood together near the fireplace. One was made of brass and the other of clay.
One day the Brass Pot said to the Clay Pot, Let us go out and see the world together!
But the Clay Pot said it was wiser to stay near the fire at home.
It takes so little to break me, he said. You know how easy it is to crack me!
Even a small bump would shatter me to pieces!
Do not let that stop you! said the Brass Pot. I will take good care of you.
If anything hard comes our way, I will step in front to protect you.
So the Clay Pot agreed, and the two set off together. They wobbled along on their short legs, bumping into each other at every step.
The poor Clay Pot could not last long in such company.
They had not even gone ten steps when the Clay Pot cracked, and the next bump smashed it into a thousand pieces.
moral: Equals make the best friends.

title: The Goose And The Golden Egg
text: Once there was a man who had a wonderful Goose. Every single day, the Goose would lay one shiny golden egg.
The man took the golden eggs to the market and soon became rich.
But before long, he grew impatient. The Goose gave him only one golden egg a day.
He wanted to get rich even faster.
One day, after counting his money, he had an idea. He would cut the Goose open and get all the golden eggs at once!
But when he did so, there was not a single golden egg inside — and his precious Goose was dead.
moral: Those who have plenty want more and so lose all they have.

title: The Fighting Bulls And The Frog
text: Two Bulls were fighting hard in a field, next to a marshy pond where some Frogs lived.
An old Frog watched the fierce battle and shook with fear.
Why are you so afraid? asked a young Frog.
Do you not see, said the old Frog, that the Bull who loses will be chased away from the good grassy field, right into our marsh? Then he will trample all of us into the mud!
And it happened just as the old Frog had said.
The losing Bull was driven into the marsh, and his great hoofs crushed many of the Frogs.
moral: When the great fall out, the weak must suffer for it.

title: The Mouse And The Weasel
text: A hungry little Mouse found a basket full of corn one day.
He had to squeeze himself very thin to get through the narrow gap in the basket.
But the corn looked so tasty that the Mouse was determined to get inside.
Once in, he ate and ate until he was very, very full.
His tummy became about three times as round as it was before!
At last he felt satisfied and went to the opening to crawl back out.
But now he was too fat to fit through!
There he sat, groaning with a full belly and worrying about how to escape.
Just then a Weasel came by. He understood at once what had happened.
My friend, said the Weasel, I can see exactly what you have been doing.
You ate too much! That is what you get.
You will have to wait there until you are as thin as when you came in.
Goodnight to you!
And that was all the kindness the poor Mouse received.
moral: Greediness leads to misfortune.

title: The Farmer And The Snake
text: A Farmer was walking through his field on a cold winter morning.
He saw a Snake lying on the ground, stiff and frozen from the cold.
The Farmer knew how dangerous the Snake could be. But he felt sorry for it, so he picked it up and kept it close to his chest to warm it.
The Snake slowly came back to life. When it was strong enough, it bit the kind man who had saved it.
The bite was deadly, and the Farmer knew he was going to die.
With his last breath, he said to those around him: Let my fate teach you — never show kindness to a wicked creature.
moral: Learn from my fate not to take pity on a scoundrel.

title: The Stick Stag
text: A Stag fell very ill one day.
He had just enough strength to gather some food and find a quiet clearing in the forest to rest and get better.
The other animals heard he was sick and came to see how he was doing.
Of course, they were all hungry, and they helped themselves to the Stag's food. Soon the poor Stag had nothing left and slowly starved.
moral: Good will is worth nothing unless it is accompanied by good acts.

title: The Goatherd And The Wild Goats
text: On a cold and stormy day, a Goatherd brought his Goats into a cave for shelter. Some Wild Goats had also come into the cave to escape the storm.
The Goatherd wanted the Wild Goats to join his flock, so he fed them very well.
But he gave his own Goats only a little food — just enough to keep them alive.
When the storm passed and the Goatherd led the Goats out to graze, the Wild Goats ran off to the hills.
Is this how you thank me for feeding you so well? complained the Goatherd.
Do not expect us to stay with you, said one of the Wild Goats. We saw how you treated your old Goats when we arrived. If others come tomorrow, you will treat us the same way.
moral: It is unwise to treat old friends badly for the sake of new ones.

title: The Spendthrift And The Swallow
text: A young man loved spending money freely and was very popular with his friends. Soon he had wasted all his money and had nothing left.
One fine day in early spring, he found himself with not a single coin, wearing only the clothes on his back.
He was supposed to meet friends that morning and desperately needed money to look good.
Just then he saw a Swallow flying by and singing happily. The young man thought summer had arrived! He rushed to a market and sold all his clothes, keeping only a thin tunic.
But a few days later, the weather turned bitterly cold. The poor Swallow shivered, and so did the foolish young man, standing there in his thin tunic with bare arms and knees.
moral: One swallow does not make a summer.

title: The Cat And The Birds
text: A Cat was getting very thin. As you might guess, he was not getting enough to eat.
One day he heard that some Birds nearby were feeling sick and needed a doctor.
So the Cat put on a pair of glasses, picked up a small bag, and knocked on the door of the Birds' home.
The Birds peeped out. Doctor Cat asked very sweetly how they were feeling.
He said he would be very happy to give them some medicine.
Tweet tweet! laughed the Birds.
Very clever, aren't you?
We are perfectly fine, thank you! And we will feel even better if you just go away!
moral: Be wise and shun the quack.

title: The Dog And The Oyster
text: Once there was a Dog who loved eggs very much.
He visited the hen house so often and became so greedy that he would swallow whole eggs in one gulp.
One day the Dog wandered down to the seashore and spotted an Oyster.
In a flash, he swallowed the Oyster — shell and all!
It hurt him very badly, as you can imagine.
I have learnt my lesson, he groaned. Not every round thing is an egg!
moral: Act in haste and repent at leisure - and often in pain.

title: The Astrologer
text: Long ago, there was a man who believed he could see the future by reading the stars.
He called himself an Astrologer and spent his nights gazing up at the sky.
One evening he was walking along the road outside his village.
His eyes were fixed on the stars above. He thought he saw signs of great danger ahead — when suddenly he fell straight into a muddy ditch!
There he stood, up to his ears in muddy water, clawing at the slippery sides trying to climb out.
His shouts for help brought the villagers running.
As they pulled him out of the mud, one of them said: You say you can read the future in the stars, yet you cannot see what is right at your feet!
This should teach you to pay attention to what is in front of you, and let the future look after itself.
What is the use, said another, of reading the stars when you cannot even see what is on the ground?
moral: Take care of the little things and the big things will take care of themselves.

title: Three Bullocks And A Lion
text: A Lion had been watching three Bullocks grazing in an open field.
He had tried to attack them many times, but they always stayed together and drove him away.
The Lion had little hope of eating them. Three strong Bullocks with sharp horns were more than a match for him.
But he could not stay away from the field. It was very hard to stop watching such a fine meal, even when he could not have it.
Then one day the Bullocks had a quarrel. When the hungry Lion came to look at them as he always did, he found them standing in different corners of the field,
as far away from each other as they could be.
Now it was easy for the Lion to attack them one by one. And that is exactly what he did, with great happiness.
moral: In unity is strength.

title: Mercury And The Woodman
text: A poor Woodcutter was chopping down a tree near a deep pool in the forest.
It was late in the evening and the Woodcutter was very tired.
He had been working since sunrise, and his arms were growing weak.
Suddenly his axe slipped from his hands and fell into the pool.
The Woodcutter was very upset.
That axe was his only way to earn a living, and he had no money to buy a new one.
As he stood there crying, the god Mercury suddenly appeared and asked what was wrong.
The Woodcutter told him what had happened, and kind Mercury dived into the pool at once.
When he came back up, he was holding a beautiful golden axe.
Is this your axe? Mercury asked.
No, said the honest Woodcutter, that is not my axe.
Mercury put the golden axe aside and dived back into the pool.
