This time he came up with a silver axe. But again the Woodcutter said that his axe was just a plain one with a wooden handle.
Mercury dived down a third time, and this time he brought up the Woodcutter's very own axe.
The poor Woodcutter was so happy and thanked Mercury again and again.
Mercury was very pleased with the man's honesty.
I am proud of your honesty, he said. As a reward, you may keep all three axes — the golden one, the silver one, and your own.
The happy Woodcutter went home with his treasures. Soon everyone in the village heard about his good fortune.
Several other Woodcutters in the village thought they could get the same reward.
They ran into the forest, hid their axes in the bushes, and pretended they had lost them.
Then they wept and called on Mercury to help them.
Mercury did appear to each one of them.
He showed each one a golden axe, and each one quickly lied and said it was his own.
But Mercury did not give them the golden axe.
Oh no! Instead, he gave each liar a hard knock on the head with it and sent them home.
And when they went back the next day to look for their own axes, they were nowhere to be found.
moral: Honesty is the best policy.

title: The Frog And The Mouse
text: A young Mouse was running along the bank of a pond, looking for adventure. A Frog lived in that pond.
When the Frog saw the Mouse, he swam to the bank and called out: Come and visit me! I promise you will have a great time!
I will show you wonderful things you have never seen before.
The Mouse was very excited to explore the world and did not need much pushing.
But though he could swim a little, he was afraid to go into the deep pond alone.
The Frog had a plan.
He tied the Mouse's leg to his own leg with a strong reed.
Then he jumped into the pond, dragging the poor Mouse along with him.
The Mouse quickly wanted to go back to the shore. But the sneaky Frog had other ideas.
He pulled the Mouse down under the water and drowned him.
But before the Frog could untie the reed from the dead Mouse, a Hawk flying above spotted the Mouse floating on the water.
The Hawk swooped down, grabbed the Mouse, and flew away — with the Frog dangling from its leg.
In one swoop, the Hawk had caught both his meal and a fish!
moral: Those who seek to harm others often come to harm themselves through their own deceit.

title: The Fox And The Crab
text: One day a Crab grew tired of the sandy beach where he lived.
He decided to crawl out to the green meadow not far away.
He thought he would find better food there than salty water and tiny sand creatures.
So off he crawled to the meadow.
But a hungry Fox spotted him there and, in no time at all, gobbled him up — shell, claws and all.
moral: Be content with your lot.

title: The Serpent And The Eagle
text: A Snake had crept up on an Eagle and wrapped itself tightly around the Eagle's neck.
The Eagle could not reach the Snake with its beak or claws.
It flew high into the sky trying to shake the Snake off.
But the Snake held on tighter and tighter, and slowly the Eagle fell back to earth, gasping for air.
A farmer passing by saw the unfair fight.
Feeling sorry for the great Eagle, he rushed over and quickly pulled the Snake away, setting the Eagle free.
The Snake was furious.
It could not bite the watchful farmer.
So instead, it struck at the farmer's drinking horn hanging at his side and poured its deadly poison inside.
The farmer continued walking toward home.
Feeling thirsty on the way, he filled his horn with water from a spring and was about to drink.
Suddenly there was a great rush of wings.
The Eagle swooped down and snatched the poisoned horn right out of the farmer's hands, and flew away with it to hide it somewhere safe forever.
moral: An act of kindness is well repaid.

title: The Wolf In Sheep'S Clothing
text: A Wolf could not get enough to eat because the Shepherds and their Dogs were always watching.
But one night he found an old sheep skin that had been left behind.
The next day, dressed in the sheep skin, the Wolf walked into the field with the flock.
Soon a little Lamb began to follow him and was quickly led away and eaten.
That evening the Wolf slipped into the sheep shed with the rest of the flock.
But that very evening, the Shepherd felt like having mutton soup for dinner. He picked up his knife and went to the shed.
The first animal he caught and killed was the Wolf himself.
moral: The evil doer often comes to harm through his own deceit.

title: The Bull And The Goat
text: A Bull once ran away from a Lion and hid in a cave that Goatherds used as shelter for their flocks.
A Goat had been left alone in the cave. As soon as the Bull entered, the Goat lowered his head and charged, butting the Bull hard with his horns.
Since the Lion was still waiting outside the cave, the Bull had to put up with it.
Do not think I am putting up with this because I am afraid of you, said the Bull.
When that Lion goes away, I will teach you a lesson you will never forget.
moral: It is wicked to take advantage of another's distress.

title: The Eagle And The Beetle
text: A Beetle once begged the Eagle not to hurt a Hare that had run to her for safety.
But the Eagle ignored the Beetle and swooped down on the Hare. The rush of her great wings sent the Beetle tumbling far away.
The Beetle was very angry at being treated so rudely. She flew to the Eagle's nest and rolled all the eggs out.
She did not spare a single one.
The Eagle was heartbroken and furious, but she did not know who had done it.
The next year the Eagle built her nest high up on a mountain rock. But the Beetle found it and again broke all the eggs.
In despair, the Eagle flew to great Jupiter and begged him to keep her eggs safe in his lap.
Surely no one would dare harm them there.
But the Beetle buzzed around Jupiter's head, making him jump up, and the eggs rolled off his lap and broke.
Then the Beetle told Jupiter why she had done all this. Jupiter agreed that the Beetle was right.
And it is said that ever since, while Eagle eggs lie in the nest in spring, the Beetle sleeps underground. For so Jupiter commanded.
moral: Even the weakest may find means to avenge a wrong.

title: The Old Lion And The Fox
text: An old Lion's teeth and claws had grown weak, and it was hard for him to find food like before. So he pretended to be very sick.
He made sure all his neighbours heard about it, then lay down in his cave and waited for visitors.
When the animals came to check on him, he ate them up one by one.
The Fox came too, but he was very careful.
He stood at a safe distance from the cave and politely asked how the Lion was feeling.
The Lion said he was very ill indeed and asked the Fox to come inside for a moment.
But the wise Fox stayed right where he was and thanked the Lion kindly for the invitation.
I would love to come in, he said, but I notice that there are many footprints going into your cave and not a single one coming out.
Could you please tell me — how do your visitors find their way out again?
moral: Take warning from the misfortunes of others.

title: The Man And The Lion
text: A Man and a Lion were walking together through the forest one day.
They soon began to argue, for each one said that he and his kind were much stronger and smarter than the other.
Soon they came to a clearing in the forest. There stood a great stone statue.
It showed a mighty hero tearing open the jaws of a Lion.
See! said the Man. That shows how strong we humans are! A Lion is like soft clay in our hands!
Ha! laughed the Lion. A Man made that statue.
If a Lion had made it, you can be sure the picture would look very different!
moral: It all depends on the point of view, and who tells the story.

title: The Ass And The Lap Dog
text: There was once a Donkey whose master also had a little pet Dog.
The Dog was a great favourite. The Master petted him, spoke kindly to him, and gave him tasty treats from his own plate.
Every day the Dog would run to greet the Master, jumping up happily to lick his hands and face.
The Donkey watched all this and felt very unhappy.
He worked hard all day, yet the Master barely noticed him.
The jealous Donkey thought he just needed to act like the Dog to win the Master's love.
So one day he left his stable and clattered noisily into the house.
He found his Master sitting at the dinner table. The Donkey kicked up his heels, brayed loudly, and pranced around the table, knocking it over.
Then he placed his heavy front legs on the Master's knees and tried to lick his face, just like the Dog did.
But the Donkey's weight toppled the chair, and both the Master and Donkey crashed to the ground among the broken dishes.
The Master shouted for help, very frightened by the Donkey's strange behaviour.
When the servants arrived and saw the Master in danger, they rushed in and beat the Donkey back to his stable.
There the Donkey was left alone to feel sorry for his foolishness, which had earned him nothing but a good thrashing.
moral: Behavior that is regarded as agreeable in one is very rude and impertinent in another.

title: The Milkmaid And Her Pail
text: A Milkmaid had finished milking the cows and was walking home with a full pail of milk balanced on her head.
As she walked, her mind was busy with happy plans for the future.
This lovely rich milk, she thought to herself, will give me plenty of cream to make butter.
I will sell the butter at the market, and with that money I will buy a lot of eggs to hatch into chicks.
How wonderful it will be when the yard is full of fluffy little chicks!
When the fair comes, I will sell the chicks and buy a beautiful new dress to wear.
All the young men will surely notice me!
They will come and try to talk to me, but I shall send them away quickly!
As she tossed her head proudly at the thought, the pail of milk tumbled from her head and crashed to the ground.
All the milk spilled out, and with it went the butter, the eggs, the chicks, the new dress — and all the milkmaid's lovely dreams.
moral: Do not count your chickens before they are hatched.

title: The Wolf And The Shepherd
text: A Wolf was hiding near the Shepherd's hut and saw the Shepherd and his family happily eating a roasted lamb.
How funny! he muttered. What a fuss they would make if they caught me doing the very same thing they are so happily doing right now!
moral: Men often condemn others for what they see no wrong in doing themselves.

title: The Goatherd And The Goat
text: A Goat wandered away from the flock, attracted by a patch of fresh green grass.
The Goatherd called and called, but the Goat would not come back.
The Goat just ignored him.
Angry and frustrated, the Goatherd threw a stone and accidentally broke the Goat's horn.
The Goatherd was frightened about what his master would say.
Please do not tell the master, he begged the Goat.
Do not worry, said the Goat calmly, this broken horn will speak for itself!
moral: Wicked deeds will not stay hid.

title: The Miser
text: A greedy Miser had hidden all his gold in a hole in his garden.
Every single day he went to the spot, dug up the gold, and counted every coin to make sure nothing was missing.
He visited so often that a Thief noticed him and guessed what was hidden there. One night the Thief quietly dug it all up and ran away.
When the Miser found his gold was gone, he was overcome with grief.
He cried, moaned, and pulled at his hair.
A passerby heard the noise and asked what had happened.
My gold! Oh, my gold! cried the Miser. Someone has stolen it!
Your gold? In that hole in the ground?
Why did you hide it there? Why not keep it in the house where you could use it to buy things?
Buy things? cried the Miser angrily.
I never once touched or spent any of the gold!
The passerby picked up a large stone and dropped it into the hole.
Well then, he said, bury this stone instead. It will do you just as much good as the gold you never used!
moral: A possession is worth no more than the use we make of it.

title: The Wolf And The House Dog
text: There was once a Wolf who could hardly find anything to eat. The village Dogs were always awake and alert.
The Wolf was thin as a stick, and it made him very sad.
One night the Wolf came across a big, fat House Dog who had strayed a little too far from home.
The Wolf would have loved to eat him right then, but the Dog looked strong enough to put up a good fight.
So the Wolf spoke to the Dog very sweetly, complimenting him on how well-fed and healthy he looked.
You can live like this too, if you want, said the Dog. Leave the forest — you live so miserably there.
You have to fight for every bite you eat.
Come with me and life will be much better for you.
What would I have to do? asked the Wolf.
Hardly anything at all, said the Dog. Chase away strangers, bark at beggars, and be friendly to the family.
In return, you will get all kinds of good food — scraps of chicken, meat, sweets, cakes, and much more! Not to mention kind words and pats.
The Wolf's eyes lit up. He almost cried with joy thinking of such a life.
But then he noticed that the fur on the Dog's neck was rubbed away and the skin was sore.
What happened to your neck? asked the Wolf.
Oh, nothing, said the Dog.
Nothing? But please tell me!
Oh, it is a small thing! It is just where my collar rubs against the chain.
What! A chain! cried the Wolf. Are you not free to go where you like?
Not always, said the Dog. But what does it matter?
It matters everything! said the Wolf. I would not trade all your feasts for my freedom. Not for all the lambs in the world!
And with that, the Wolf ran back to the forest.
moral: There is nothing worth so much as liberty.

title: The Fox And The Hedgehog
text: A Fox was swimming across a river and barely made it to the bank. He lay there bruised and exhausted from fighting the strong current.
Soon a swarm of flies settled on him and began to bite. But he was too weak to drive them away.
A Hedgehog happened to come by.
Let me chase those flies away for you, said the Hedgehog kindly.
No, no! said the Fox. Please do not disturb them!
These flies have already drunk their fill. If you drive them away, a fresh, hungry swarm will come and drink up all the little blood I have left!
moral: Better to bear a lesser evil than to risk a greater in removing it.

title: The Bat And The Weasels
text: A Bat stumbled into the nest of a Weasel, who rushed at him to catch and eat him.
The Bat begged for his life, but the Weasel refused to listen.
You are a Mouse, said the Weasel, and I am the sworn enemy of all mice.
Every mouse I catch, I eat!
But I am not a Mouse! cried the Bat.
Look at my wings!
Can mice fly?
I am a Bird!
Please let me go!
The Weasel had to agree that the Bat was not a Mouse, so he let him go.
But a few days later, the foolish Bat bumbled into the nest of another Weasel.
This Weasel was the enemy of all birds, and he quickly grabbed the Bat and was about to eat him.
You are a Bird, he said, and I am going to eat you!
What? Me, a Bird? cried the Bat.
All birds have feathers!
I am nothing but a plain Mouse.
I am on the side of all mice, not birds!
And so the clever Bat escaped with his life a second time.
moral: Set your sails with the wind.

title: The Quack Toad
text: An old Toad told all his neighbours that he was a great doctor and could cure any illness.
The Fox heard this news and quickly went to see the Toad.
He looked the Toad over carefully from head to toe. Mr. Toad, said the Fox, I hear you can cure everything!
But take a good look at yourself first. Try some of your own medicine!
If you can cure your own patchy skin and your stiff, slow walk, then perhaps someone might believe you.
Otherwise, dear Toad, I think you should find a different job.
moral: Those who would mend others, should first mend themselves.

title: The Fox Without A Tail
text: A Fox was once caught in a trap. After a long and painful struggle, he finally managed to get free.
But he had to leave his beautiful bushy tail behind in the trap.
For a long time, he stayed away from the other Foxes. He knew they would laugh at him and make fun of his missing tail.
But living alone was hard, so at last he came up with a plan to help himself.
He called a big meeting of all the Foxes, saying he had something very important to share.
When they were all gathered, the Fox Without a Tail stood up and gave a long speech about how dangerous tails were.
One fox, he said, had been caught by hunting dogs because his tail got stuck in a bush.
Another could not run fast because his tail was too heavy.
And everyone knows, he added, that hunters chase foxes just to cut off their tails as trophies.
With all this proof, said the Fox, he strongly advised every fox to cut off his tail for his own safety.
When he finished, an old Fox stood up and smiled. Dear friend, he said, please turn around for a moment, and we will give you our answer.
When the poor Fox Without a Tail turned around, all the other Foxes burst into loud laughter and jeers. He realised it was no use trying to trick them into cutting off their tails.
moral: Do not listen to the advice of him who seeks to lower you to his own level.

title: The Mischievous Dog
text: A naughty dog troubled everyone, so his master tied a wooden block to his neck.
The proud dog dragged the noisy block around to show off to everybody.
But nobody in the village was impressed by him.
An old dog said, "You should hide quietly with that wooden block."
"Do you want everyone to know how badly you behave?"
moral: Notoriety is not fame.

title: The Rose And The Butterfly
text: Once, a pretty butterfly fell in love with a lovely red rose.
The rose liked him too, because his wings had shiny gold and silver patterns.
When he fluttered close and said he loved her, the rose blushed and smiled.
They promised to stay true to each other, and then the butterfly flew away.
But many days passed, and the butterfly did not come back for a long time.
"Did you forget your promise?" the rose cried when he finally returned.
"You stayed away so long, dancing with all the other garden flowers!"
"I saw you kissing other flowers until a big bee chased you away!"
"I really wish that big bee had stung you!"
"My promise?" laughed the butterfly. "The gentle wind was kissing your petals too!"
"You smiled at buzzing bumblebees and winked at every passing beetle in the garden!"
"If you are not faithful, you cannot expect me to be faithful either!"
moral: Do not expect constancy in others if you have none yourself.

title: The Cat And The Fox
text: Once, a cat and a fox were walking through the forest together.
As they hunted for tasty food, they started arguing to pass the time.
Soon, like friends who argue, they began boasting about themselves.
"You think you are very clever, don't you?" sneered the proud fox.
"Do you really think you are smarter than me?"
"Why, I know a whole bag full of clever tricks!"
"Well," said the cat, "I only know one trick, but it is worth a thousand!"
Suddenly, they heard the loud barks of a hunter's pack of hunting dogs.
In a flash, the cat scrambled up a mango tree and hid in the leaves.
"This is my only trick!" called the cat to the fox below.
"Now let us see your clever tricks at work!"
But the fox had so many plans that he could not pick one.
He ran left and right, but the hunting dogs stayed right behind him.
He jumped into holes and ran in circles, but nothing helped him escape.
The dogs caught the boasting fox, putting an end to all his tricks.
moral: Common sense is always worth more than cunning.

title: The Boy And The Nettles
text: A little boy was stung by a prickly weed and ran crying to his mother.
His mother said, "Hold it firmly next time, and it will feel like soft silk."
moral: Whatever you do, do with all your might.

title: The Old Lion
text: A mighty lion had grown very old and weak.
His sharp teeth were all worn away.
His legs could not carry him, and the old king lay helpless on the ground.
All his great power and handsome strength were gone now.
A wild boar saw him, charged forward, and struck him with sharp tusks.
A heavy bull rushed up and stamped on him with hard hooves.
Even a silly donkey kicked the lion and brayed rude words into his face.
moral: It is cowardly to attack the defenseless, though he be an enemy.

title: The Fox And The Pheasants
text: One moonlit night, a sly fox saw birds sitting high on a tall tree branch.
The fox stood in the bright moonlight and began to dance on his back legs.
He spun around like a top and hopped up and down with silly jumps.
The birds watched him, feeling very dizzy.
They did not even dare to blink because they could not look away.
The fox pretended to climb, played dead, and wiggled his bushy tail in the moonlight.
Soon, the poor birds were completely confused and dizzy.
When the fox danced again, the dizzy birds fell off the branch one by one.
moral: Too much attention to danger may cause us to fall victims to it.

title: Two Travelers And A Bear
text: Two friends were walking through a forest when a huge bear suddenly appeared.
One man only thought of himself and quickly climbed up a tree.
The other man could not fight alone, so he fell down and played dead.
He had heard that bears never touch a dead body.
The bear sniffed his face, thought he was dead, and quietly walked away.
The first man climbed down from the tree with a smile.
"It looked like the bear whispered a secret in your ear," he said.
"What did that big bear say to you?"
The other replied, "Never trust a friend who leaves you alone in danger."
moral: Misfortune is the test of true friendship.

title: The Porcupine And The Snakes
text: A porcupine was searching the forest for a warm home.
At last, he found a cozy little cave where a family of snakes lived.
He asked to share their cave, and the kind snakes happily agreed.
But the snakes soon regretted letting their new guest move in.
His sharp needles pricked them everywhere, so they politely asked him to leave.
"I am very comfortable here, thank you," said the porcupine with a grin.
"I will stay right here," he said, pushing the snakes out of the cave.
To protect themselves from his sharp quills, the poor snakes had to find another home.
moral: Give a finger and lose a hand.

title: The Fox And The Monkey
text: The jungle animals gathered to choose a king, and the monkey danced for them.
He made such funny jumps and faces that the happy animals crowned him king.
The wise fox was upset that the animals chose such a silly ruler.
One day, the fox found a hunter's trap with a tasty piece of meat inside.
He told the monkey king he had found a delicious royal treat for him.
The greedy monkey followed the fox straight to the trap.
He grabbed the meat greedily, and snap! The trap caught him tight.
The fox laughed loudly from a safe distance.
"You want to be our king, yet you cannot even keep yourself safe!" he said.
Soon after that, the animals held another meeting to choose a wiser king.
moral: The true leader proves himself by his qualities.

title: The Mother And The Wolf
text: One morning, a hungry wolf near a village hut heard a child crying inside.
Then he heard the mother say, "Hush, little one, stop crying!"
"If you do not stop, I will give you to the big bad wolf!"
Delighted by this easy meal, the wolf waited happily under the open window.
The baby kept crying, but the wolf waited all day for nothing.
At sunset, the mother rocked her baby gently by the window and began to sing.
"Do not cry, sweet baby, the wolf will never hurt you!"
"Your father is here, and he will chase the wolf far away!"
Just then, the father returned with his dogs, and the frightened wolf ran away fast.
moral: Do not believe everything you hear.

title: The Flies And The Honey
text: A clay pot of sweet honey tipped over, spilling all across the kitchen table.
The sweet smell quickly brought a swarm of buzzing flies into the room.
The flies did not wait for anyone to invite them.
They landed greedily on the sweet puddle and began eating as much as they could.
Soon, the flies were covered in thick, sticky honey from head to foot.
Their wings got stuck tightly together.
They tried to fly, but their tiny feet could not pull free from the goo.
Sadly, the greedy flies died just because they could not resist a sweet taste.
moral: Be not greedy for a little passing pleasure. It may destroy you.

title: The Eagle And The Kite
text: A majestic eagle sat on a tall banyan tree, looking very sad and lonely.
Her feathers drooped as she stared at the ground below.
A kite saw her and asked, "Why do you look so sad and gloomy?"
asked the kite as he flew down beside her.
"I want to marry, but I cannot find a mate who can feed me well."
"Marry me!" said the kite. "I am stronger even than you!"
"Can you really hunt big food for me?" asked the eagle eagerly.
"Why, of course I can!" replied the kite with a proud nod.
"Catching big animals is very easy for me."
"I am so strong that I can carry a giant ostrich like a feather!"
Delighted by his big words, the eagle agreed to marry him right away.
After the wedding, the kite flew off and returned with only a tiny dead mouse.
"Is this the giant ostrich you promised me?" cried the angry eagle.
"I only said those big words so you would marry me," confessed the kite.
moral: Everything is fair in love.

title: The Stag, The Sheep, And The Wolf
text: One day, a deer came to a sheep and asked to borrow some wheat.
The sheep knew the deer could run very fast and easily vanish into the forest.
So the sheep asked, "Is there someone trustworthy who will promise to pay for you?"
"Yes, indeed!" said the deer proudly. "The big wolf will promise for me."
"The wolf!" cried the sheep in horror and disbelief.
"Do you really think I would trust a promise from a wolf?"
"The wolf always steals what he wants and runs away without paying anything!"
"And you run so fast that I could never catch you to get it back!"
moral: Two blacks do not make a white.

title: The Animals And The Plague
text: Long ago, a terrible sickness spread among all the animals in the forest.
Many died, and the sick ones were too weak to eat or walk.
Even the sly fox and greedy wolf did not feel like hunting any food.
At last, the lion king called a big meeting of all the forest animals.
The lion said, "Friends, heaven has sent this sickness to punish our bad deeds."
"The guiltiest animal among us must be offered to the gods."
"Only then will our sickness be cured, and we will all be saved."
"I will be the first to confess all my bad deeds."
"I have been very greedy and have eaten many harmless sheep."
"Those poor sheep never did anything wrong to me."
"I have also hunted and eaten many goats, bulls, and deer."
"To be honest, I even attacked and ate a village shepherd sometimes."
"If I am the worst sinner, I am ready to give my life."
"But each of you must also confess your bad deeds like me."
"Then we can choose fairly who is the most guilty one."
The sly fox bowed and said, "Your Majesty, you are far too kind!"
"How could eating silly sheep ever be a crime for a king?"
"Not at all, dear King Lion!"
"You actually honored those foolish sheep by eating them up!"
"And as for shepherds, those silly humans always pretend to rule over us!"
All the other animals cheered loudly and clapped for the fox's speech.
The tiger, bear, and wolf told their wicked deeds, but everyone excused them.
Next, it was the gentle donkey's turn to speak up.
The donkey whispered, "Once, I was hungry and nibbled grass from a farmer's field."
"I had no right to eat it," he began, but the beasts roared in anger.
"Here is the wicked villain who brought this sickness upon us all!"
"What an awful crime it is to steal grass from a poor farmer!"
"A donkey who steals grass surely deserves the worst punishment!"
The wild animals pounced on the poor donkey together and killed him at once.
moral: The weak are made to suffer for the misdeeds of the powerful.

title: The Shepherd And The Lion
text: A shepherd counted his sheep one day and found that several were missing.
Very angry, he loudly boasted that he would catch the thief and beat him.
Suspecting a wolf, he marched into the rocky hills where wolves lived in caves.
He prayed to the king of gods, promising a calf if he found the thief.
Suddenly, near a mountain cave, a huge lion stepped out carrying a sheep.
Trembling with fear, the poor shepherd fell to his knees on the rocks.
"O king of gods, we truly do not know what we ask for!"
"I promised a fat calf if you helped me find this thief."
"Now I promise a giant bull if you just make the thief go away!"
moral: We are often not so eager for what we seek, after we have found it.

title: The Dog And His Reflection
text: A dog got a juicy bone and ran happily toward home with his prize.
As he crossed a small wooden bridge, he looked down into the clear stream.
He saw his reflection and thought it was another dog with a bigger bone.
The silly dog did not stop to think for even a single second.
He barked greedily to grab the bone, and his own piece fell into the river.
As he stood shivering and wet on the riverbank, he felt very foolish indeed.
moral: It is very foolish to be greedy.

title: The Hare And The Tortoise
text: One day, a speedy hare made fun of a tortoise for walking so slowly.
"Do you ever reach anywhere on time?" asked the hare with a rude laugh.
"Yes, I do," said the tortoise, "and faster than you think."
"Let us run a race, and I will prove it to you."
The hare laughed loudly at the funny idea, but agreed to the race.
The wise fox agreed to judge, marked the finish line, and started the race.
The hare zoomed far ahead, then lay down under a tree to take a nap.
Meanwhile, the tortoise walked on slowly, step by step, without ever stopping to rest.
The hare slept deeply while the slow tortoise quietly walked right past him.
When the hare finally woke up and ran fast, the tortoise had already won!
moral: The race is not always to the swift.

title: The Bees And Wasps, And The Hornet
text: Sweet honey was found in a hollow tree, and the wasps claimed it was theirs.
The honeybees were just as sure that the sweet honey belonged to them.
They argued loudly and were about to fight, but decided to consult a judge instead.
They brought their case before Judge Hornet, the head of the forest court.
Witnesses said they saw yellow and black striped insects flying around the tree.
The wasps quickly shouted that they also had yellow and black stripes.
Judge Hornet could not decide, so he delayed the court for six long weeks.
When court reopened, both sides brought many witnesses to speak for them.
Before an ant could speak, a wise old honeybee stood up in court.
"Sir," said the bee, "this case has gone on for six whole weeks."
"If we wait any longer, all the sweet honey will get spoiled."
"Let the wasps and bees each build a new honeycomb right now."
"Then everyone can see who can truly make this sweet honey."
The wasps buzzed with fear and loudly refused to build any comb.
Wise Judge Hornet knew right away that wasps could never make real honeycombs.
"It is very clear who made this sweet treasure," declared Judge Hornet.
"All this delicious honey belongs to the hard-working bees!"
moral: Ability proves itself by deeds.

title: The Lark And Her Young Ones
text: A mother lark built her cozy nest in a field of green wheat.
As the wheat grew tall, her baby chicks grew stronger each day.
One sunny day, the farmer and his son walked into the golden field.
"The wheat is ripe," said the farmer to his young son.
"We must ask our neighbors and friends to help us harvest the crop."
The baby chicks were terrified, fearing the workers would crush their nest.
When their mother flew back with food, they told her what they heard.
"Do not worry, little ones," said the wise mother bird gently.
"If the farmer waits for neighbors, the wheat will not be cut yet."
A few days later, the grains were falling softly onto their heads.
The farmer cried, "We cannot wait for friends, or our crop will spoil!"
"Nobody came to help us harvest this field."
"Tomorrow, we will harvest all the wheat with our own hands!"
When the chicks told their mother, she said, "Now we must fly away!"
"When a person does his own work, things happen without any delay."
The chicks flapped their wings and flew safely away before the morning harvest.
moral: Self-help is the best help.

title: The Cat And The Old Rat
text: A sharp cat was so watchful that mice rarely dared to show their whiskers.
The cat seemed to be everywhere, ready to pounce with sharp claws.
When the mice hid safely inside their holes, the cat planned a trick.
He hung upside down from a rope, pretending to be completely dead.
The mice looked out and thought someone had punished the naughty cat.
Slowly, the little mice poked their noses out and sniffed the room.
Seeing no movement, they danced out happily to celebrate the cat's end.
Suddenly, the cat dropped down and caught three or four foolish mice.
After that scary day, the mice stayed strictly inside their dark holes.
But the hungry cat still had another clever trick up his sleeve.
He rolled in white flour and hid quietly inside the kitchen flour box.
Soon, the young mice began creeping out to search for food again.
But a wise old rat, who had once lost his tail, watched carefully.
"Watch out!" warned the old rat from the safety of his hole.
"That looks like a pile of flour, but it is really the tricky cat!"
moral: The wise do not let themselves be tricked a second time.

title: The Fox And The Crow
text: One morning, a hungry fox walked through the woods looking for food.
He looked up and saw a black crow sitting on a tree branch.
In her beak, the lucky crow was holding a tasty piece of cheese.
"My search is over," thought the sly fox with a greedy smile.
"That delicious cheese will make a wonderful breakfast for me!"
He trotted to the tree and called out, "Good morning, beautiful bird!"
The crow tilted her head and looked down at him very suspiciously.
She kept her beak clamped tightly shut on the yummy cheese.
"Look how your shiny black feathers sparkle in the bright morning sun!" said the fox.
"A bird so beautiful must surely have the sweetest singing voice too!"
"If you sing for me, I will crown you the Queen of Birds!"
Hearing such sweet praise, the foolish crow forgot all about her caution.
She really wanted to be called the Queen of all Birds.
She opened her beak wide to caw, and the cheese dropped right down!
The fox swallowed it and laughed, "You have a voice, but no brains!"
moral: The flatterer lives at the expense of those who will listen to him.

title: The Ass And His Shadow
text: A traveler hired a donkey to carry him to a far-off town.
The donkey's owner walked alongside them to guide the donkey along the path.
Their dusty road crossed an open plain under the blazing hot sun.
The traveler was so hot that he sat in the donkey's shadow to rest.
The tired owner was burning hot too, because he had walked on foot all day.
He argued angrily, claiming the traveler only hired the donkey, not its shadow.
While the two foolish men fought, the donkey ran away and left them behind.
moral: In quarreling about the shadow we often lose the substance.

title: The Miller, His Son, And The Ass
text: A miller and his son took their donkey to the village market to sell him.
They walked slowly so the donkey would stay fresh and look healthy.
Passing travelers laughed loudly when they saw the two walking on foot.
"How silly!" one traveler shouted. "Why walk when you have a donkey to ride?"
Hearing this, the miller felt foolish for walking beside the animal.
So the miller lifted his young son onto the donkey's back.
Soon, three merchants walked by and shook their heads in anger.
"What a lazy boy!" shouted the passing merchants on the road.
"Show respect to elders! Get down and let your old father ride!"
The miller told his son to walk, and rode the donkey himself.
Next, they met some village women carrying baskets of fresh vegetables.
"Look at that lazy father riding while his poor little boy walks!" one cried.
Feeling upset, the miller pulled his son up onto the donkey behind him.
Then, a group of travelers saw both of them on the donkey's back.
"How cruel!" they yelled. "You are overloading that poor little animal!"
"You two look strong enough to carry the poor donkey yourselves!"
"They must be working the poor beast to death!" another said.
Confused, they tied the donkey to a pole and carried him on their shoulders.
The villagers in the crowded market laughed loudly at this funny sight.
Scared by the noise, the donkey kicked hard and snapped the ropes.
He tumbled off the bridge and splashed right into the deep river!
By trying to please everyone, the miller pleased nobody and lost his donkey too.
moral: If you try to please all, you please none.

title: The Ant And The Dove
text: A gentle dove saw a tiny ant fall into a rushing stream.
The poor ant struggled, so the kind dove dropped a dry leaf into the water.
The ant climbed onto the floating leaf and sailed safely to the riverbank.
Soon after, the ant saw a hunter aiming a stone at the resting dove.
The ant bit the hunter's heel, making him miss, and the dove flew to safety.
moral: A kindness is never wasted.

title: The Man And The Satyr
text: Long ago, a man met a woodland spirit in the forest and became friends.
The two became good companions and lived together in the man's hut.
One chilly evening, the spirit saw the man blowing on his cold fingers.
"Why are you blowing on your fingers?" asked the woodland spirit.
"I blow to warm my cold hands," the man answered with a smile.
At home, the man cooked two warm bowls of hot sweet porridge.
The two friends sat down at the table to enjoy their warm dinner.
To the spirit's surprise, the man began blowing onto his hot bowl.
"Why are you blowing on your food now?" asked the curious spirit.
"I blow to cool my hot porridge down," replied the man.
The woodland spirit jumped up from his chair and rushed to the door.
"Goodbye!" shouted the spirit. "I cannot stay here any longer!"
"I will never trust someone who blows hot and cold with the same breath!"
moral: The man who talks for both sides is not to be trusted by either.

title: The Wolf, The Kid, And The Goat
text: One morning, Mother Goat got ready to visit the village market for groceries.
"Lock the door and stay safe inside, my dear child," warned Mother Goat.
"Open only if you hear our secret password: 'Down with all hungry wolves!'"
A sneaky wolf was hiding behind a bush and heard every single word.
As soon as the mother left, the wolf trotted up and knocked.
"Down with all hungry wolves," said the wolf in a soft, pretend voice.
The password was correct, but the smart little kid peeked through a crack.
"Show me your white paw, or you cannot enter," said the careful kid.
The wolf had dark paws and slunk away, leaving the clever kid safe inside.
moral: Two sureties are better than one.

title: The Swallow And The Crow
text: One day, a swallow and a crow argued about who had prettier feathers.
The swallow boasted, "Look at my bright, soft feathers dancing in the air."
"Your stiff black feathers look plain, ugly, and totally boring!"
"Why do you not dress in colorful feathers like me?"
The crow replied, "Your feathers suit spring, but my warm coat protects me all winter!"
moral: Friends in fine weather only, are not worth much.

title: Jupiter And The Monkey
text: The forest animals held a grand contest to find the cutest baby animal.
The king of the gods promised a wonderful golden prize to the winner.
Proud animal mothers from all across the jungle arrived with their little babies.
Mother Monkey arrived early, proudly carrying her tiny baby in her arms.
She showed her little baby to the judges with a bright, happy smile.
The other animals laughed loudly at the funny-looking, flat-nosed little baby monkey.
"Laugh all you want!" said Mother Monkey, holding her baby very close.
"Even without a prize, my baby is the sweetest and dearest darling in the world!"
moral: Mother love is blind.

title: The Lion, The Ass, And The Fox
text: A lion, a donkey, and a fox went hunting together and caught plenty of meat.
The lion asked the donkey to divide the food into three fair, equal shares.
Furious at getting an equal share, the angry lion struck the poor donkey dead.
Then the roaring lion turned to the fox and ordered him to divide it.
The clever fox did not waste a single second arguing with the beast.
He piled almost all the meat into one giant heap for the lion.
For himself, the fox only kept a few tiny scraps and animal hooves.
The greedy lion smiled warmly, delighted with his huge mountain of food.
"Who taught you to divide the feast so wisely?" asked the smiling lion.
"I learned it from the poor donkey," whispered the fox, backing safely away.
moral: Learn from the misfortunes of others.

title: The Lion'S Share
text: A lion, a fox, a jackal, and a wolf agreed to hunt and share fairly.
The wolf caught a deer and called his hunting partners to share the feast.
The greedy lion stood up tall to divide the deer among all four animals.
"One is myself, King Lion," he said, tapping his sharp claws on the ground.
"Two is the wolf, three is the jackal, and four is the fox."
The lion carefully sliced the deer into four equal parts on the grass.
"Because I am the king of the jungle, the first part is mine," he said.
"The second is mine for being strongest, and the third for being bravest!"
Then the lion flashed his sharp teeth and glared fiercely at his friends.
"Whoever wants the last piece," he growled, "must fight me for it right now!"
moral: Might makes right.

title: The Mole And His Mother
text: A little mole said, "Mother, you say I am blind, but I can see!"
Mother Mole knew she had to teach her boasting little son a gentle lesson.
She placed a piece of sweet-smelling incense before him and asked what it was.
The little mole squinted close and said, "Why, that is just a hard pebble!"
"My child," sighed his mother, "you cannot see, and you cannot even smell either!"
moral: Boast of one thing and you will be found lacking in that and a few other things as well.

title: The North Wind And The Sun
text: The cold wind and the warm sun argued about who was stronger.
Just then, a traveler walked down the village road wearing a warm cloak.
"Whoever can make him take off his cloak is the winner," said the sun.
"Agreed!" howled the wind, blowing an icy storm straight at the traveler.
The harsh wind blew wildly, whipping the cloak all around the shivering man.
But the traveler only wrapped his cloak tighter and held on with all his might.
The cold wind blew harder and harder, but could not remove the cloak.
Then, the bright sun began to shine down gently with pleasant golden light.
Feeling cozy and warm, the traveler soon loosened his thick cloak with a smile.
The sun shone brighter, making the air pleasantly warm and sunny.
Soon, the traveler began sweating and wiped his forehead under the bright sky.
He took off his cloak completely and rested happily beneath a shady banyan tree.
moral: Gentleness and kind persuasion win where force and bluster fail.

title: The Hare And His Ears
text: The lion was hurt by the sharp horns of a goat he was attacking.
Furious, the king of the jungle declared that no animal should have dangerous horns.
He ordered every horned animal to leave the forest before the next morning.
The lion's strict order terrified all the creatures across the whole jungle.
Deer, bulls, and goats packed their things and prepared to leave their homes.
Even the timid hare, who had no horns, spent a sleepless, fearful night.
In the morning, the hare saw the long, pointy shadows of his own ears.
"Goodbye, friend cricket, I must run away too!" shouted the frightened hare.
"The fierce lion will surely call my long ears horns, whatever I say!"
moral: Your enemies will seize any excuse to attack you.

title: The Wolves And The Sheep
text: A pack of hungry wolves waited near the grassy meadow where sheep grazed.
But brave guard dogs protected the meadow, keeping all the gentle sheep safe.
So the sneaky wolves came up with a wicked plan to fool the sheep.
"Why must we always fight like bitter enemies?" asked the cunning wolves sweetly.
"Those loud dogs are the real troublemakers who keep us from being friends."
"Send the dogs away, and we can live together in wonderful peace."
The foolish sheep believed the sweet lies and sent their trusty dogs away.
With no dogs to protect them, the hungry wolves attacked and ate the sheep.
moral: Do not give up friends for foes.

title: The Fox And The Cock
text: One morning, a sly fox got trapped while sneaking near the farmer's chicken coop.
He was hungry, but stealing the farmer's birds was still very wrong.
A rooster woke up early and saw the trapped fox struggling on the ground.
Knowing he was safe, the rooster walked closer to look at his enemy.
The sneaky fox saw one small chance to save himself from trouble.
"Dear friend," cried the fox, "I was visiting a sick aunt and got tangled here!"
"Please do not tell the farmer about my silly little accident."
"I do not want to worry anyone, and I will chew myself free soon."
But the clever rooster was not fooled by the fox's sweet lies.
He crowed loudly, waking the farmer, who ran out and caught the naughty fox.
moral: The wicked deserve no aid.

title: The Ass In The Lion'S Skin
text: A donkey found a lion's skin left behind in the jungle by a hunter.
He wore the skin and jumped out of bushes to scare passing animals.
Every creature ran away in fright the moment they saw him coming.
Delighted by his power, the proud donkey let out a loud, noisy bray!
A running fox stopped in his tracks as soon as he heard that voice.
The fox walked over and laughed, "You might have scared me in that skin."
"But your silly donkey bray gave your foolish secret away at once!"
moral: A fool may deceive by his dress and appearance, but his words will soon show what he really is.

title: The Fisherman And The Little Fish
text: A poor village fisherman cast his net all day and caught only one tiny fish.
As he picked it up, the tiny fish begged, "Please throw me back, kind fisherman!"
"I am too small to make a good meal for your family today."
"Let me grow big in the river, and then you can catch me again!"
But the wise fisherman dropped the little fish straight into his clay pot.
"I would be very foolish to let you go back into the river," he said.
"A tiny fish in hand is far better than a big fish that gets away."
moral: A small gain is worth more than a large promise.

title: The Fighting Cocks And The Eagle
text: Two proud roosters lived in the same village courtyard and fought all the time.
One afternoon, they flew at each other with sharp beaks and claws.
They fought fiercely until one got hurt and hid quietly in a dark corner.
The winning rooster flew onto the rooftop, flapping his wings and crowing boastfully.
A hungry eagle heard the loud boast, swooped down, and carried the rooster away.
Seeing this, the other rooster stepped out safely to rule the courtyard in peace.
moral: Pride goes before a fall.
